label: D: k_rigidity
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{D: k_rigidity}
             We call a probability measure $\Lambda$ on $\mathcal{P}(E)$ $k$-rigid when it is the unique such probability measure that has its $k$th moment measure equal to $\mathcal{M}_k(\Lambda)$. Equivalently, $\Lambda$ is $k$-rigid if $\mathcal{M}_k(\Lambda) = \mathcal{M}_k(\Gamma)$ and $\Gamma \in \mathcal{P}(\mathcal{P}(E))$ implies $\Lambda = \Gamma$.
head: environment
name: $k$-rigidity

title: Remark
body_md:
By the de Finetti-Hewitt-Savage Theorem \cite[Theorem 1.1]{kallenberg05}, $k$-rigidity is equivalent to uniqueness of the infinite exchangeable extension of the corresponding $k$-coordinate law.
            Note also that $k$-rigidity of $\Lambda$ implies $k'$-rigidity of $\Lambda$ for all $k' \geq k$. An important consequence of $k$-rigidity is that it is easy to check convergence of measures to a $k$-rigid law. To be precise, suppose $\Lambda$ is $k$-rigid. Then a sequence $\Lambda_n$ of elements of $\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{P}(E))$ converges weakly to $\Lambda$ if and only if $\mathcal{M}_k(\Lambda_n)$ converges weakly to $\mathcal{M}_k(\Lambda)$.

            To justify this assertion, continuity of $\mu\mapsto\mu^{\otimes k}$
            gives the forward implication. For the converse, assume $k\geq1$.
            Marginalization gives tightness of $\mathcal{M}_1(\Lambda_n)$. For
            $\varepsilon>0$, choose compact sets $K_j\subset E$ such that
            $\sup_n\mathcal{M}_1(\Lambda_n)(K_j^c)\leq\varepsilon2^{-j}/j$.
            Markov's inequality and a union bound show that
            $\Lambda_n(\mathcal K_\varepsilon)\geq1-\varepsilon$ for every $n$,
            where
            \begin{equation*}
                \mathcal K_\varepsilon
                :=\{\mu\in\mathcal{P}(E):\mu(K_j)\geq1-1/j\text{ for every }j\geq1\}.
            \end{equation*}
            This is a closed tight subset of $\mathcal{P}(E)$, hence compact by
            Prokhorov's theorem. Thus $(\Lambda_n)$ is tight. Every
            subsequential limit $\Gamma$ satisfies
            $\mathcal{M}_k(\Gamma)=\mathcal{M}_k(\Lambda)$ by continuity, and $k$-rigidity
            gives $\Gamma=\Lambda$. Therefore $\Lambda_n$ converges weakly
            to $\Lambda$. The case $k=0$ is immediate, since $0$-rigidity
            forces $\mathcal{P}(E)$ to be a singleton.

label: E: completeness
title: Definition

name: Completeness property

title: Remark
body_md:
The completeness condition~\eqref{E: completeness} is a form of conditional
            completeness familiar from nonparametric identification.
            Newey and Powell~\cite{NeweyPowell2003} use conditional
            completeness to characterize identification in instrumental
            variable models; the precise $L^2$ formulation relevant here
            is discussed by Andrews~\cite[Section~2]{Andrews2017}.
            To make the connection explicit, let $(U,V)$ have joint law
            $\nu(du)P_u(dv)$ on an auxiliary probability space.
            Lemma~\ref{L: Kh_dense} identifies \eqref{E: completeness}
            with conditional $L^2$ completeness of $U$ given $V$.
            Thus completeness concerns the conditional law of the parameter
            $U$ given the observation $V$, and depends on the mixing law
            $\nu$. 
            
            This differs from completeness of the statistical family $(P_y)$
            in the usual sense; see
            \cite[Section~1]{KaganMalinovskyMattner2015}.
            That condition tests functions on the observation space $E$
            through their expectations under every $P_y$, whereas
            \eqref{E: completeness} tests functions on the parameter space
            $Y$ relative to the fixed mixing law $\nu$.

label: P: sharpness
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{P: sharpness}
            Let \(\Pi\) be a probability measure on \([0,\infty)\). The
            rotatable extension $\int_0^\infty \gamma_v^{\infty} d\Pi(v)$ of
            \begin{equation*}
                \mathcal{L}\left(X_1,X_2\right)
                =\int_0^\infty\gamma_v^{\otimes2}\,d\Pi\left(v\right)
            \end{equation*}
            is its unique infinite exchangeable extension if and only if the
            restriction of \(\Pi\) to \(\left(0,\infty\right)\) is zero or is
            supported on one point. Otherwise the same spherical pair has a
            nonrotatable infinite exchangeable extension.

label: T: energy_radial_extendibility
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{T: energy_radial_extendibility}
            The law $Q_d$ has an infinite exchangeable extension if and
            only if $F$ is completely monotone on $(0,\infty)$. In this
            case there is a unique finite positive measure $\mu$ on
            $(0,\infty)$ such that
            \begin{equation*}
                F(t)=\int_{(0,\infty)}e^{-\beta t}\,d\mu(\beta),
                \quad t\geq0.
            \end{equation*}
            The measure $\nu_d$ defined by
            \begin{equation}\label{E: radial_mixing_law}
                d\nu_d(\beta)=Z(\beta)^d\,d\mu(\beta)
            \end{equation}
            is a probability measure, and
            $Q_d=\int_{(0,\infty)}P_\beta^{\otimes d}\,d\nu_d(\beta)$.
            Conditionally iid sampling from $P_A$, with $A\sim\nu_d$,
            therefore gives an exchangeable extension. For $d\geq3$, this
            extension is unique. For $d=2$, it is unique if and only if
            $\nu_2$ is a point mass, equivalently, if and only if
            $F(t)=ce^{-bt}$ for some $c,b>0$.

body_md:
\label{C: lq_phase_diagram}

                \item[(a)] If $0<q<1$, then $Q_{q,d,\lambda}$ has no

                    $d$ iid Laplace random variables with rate $\lambda$,

                    exchangeable extension. It is unique if $d\geq3$ and
                    not unique if $d=2$.

label: L: Kh_dense
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Suppose that $f\in L^2(\nu)$ is orthogonal to every
            $K_h$. Since $\nu$ is a probability measure,
            $f\in L^1(\nu)$. For every bounded Borel measurable map $h$,
            Fubini's theorem gives
            \begin{equation*}
                \int_E h\,dQ_\nu[f]
                =\int_Y f(y)P_y(h)\,d\nu(y)=0,
            \end{equation*}
            so $Q_\nu[f]=0$. Conversely, if $Q_\nu[f]=0$, the same
            identity shows that $f$ is orthogonal to every $K_h$.
            Thus the orthogonal complement of their span is the kernel
            of $Q_\nu$, which proves the equivalence of the first two
            conditions.

            To compare with the third condition, put $q:=Q_\nu[\mathbf1]$,
            the law of $V$. Then $Q_\nu[f]\ll q$: if $q(C)=0$, positivity
            gives $P_y(C)=0$ for $\nu$-almost every $y$, and hence
            $Q_\nu[f](C)=0$. Let $r_f:=dQ_\nu[f]/dq$. For every bounded
            Borel measurable $h:E\to\mathbb R$,
            \begin{equation*}
                \mathbb E[f(U)h(V)]
                =\int_E h\,dQ_\nu[f]
                =\mathbb E[r_f(V)h(V)].
            \end{equation*}
            Consequently,
            \begin{equation*}
                \frac{dQ_\nu[f]}{dQ_\nu[\mathbf1]}(V)
                =\mathbb E[f(U)\mid V]
                \quad\text{almost surely}.
            \end{equation*}
            Therefore $Q_\nu[f]=0$ if and only if
            $\mathbb E[f(U)\mid V]=0$ almost surely, proving the remaining
            equivalence.

label: L: moment_isometry
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
(a) Integrating $h\otimes h'$ against both sides of the second
            moment identity gives
            \begin{equation*}
                \mathbb E[\eta(h)\eta(h')]
                =\int_Y K_hK_{h'}\,d\nu
                =\left\langle K_h,K_{h'}\right\rangle_{L^2(\nu)}.
            \end{equation*}
            Applying this to $h-h'$ and using linearity,
            \begin{equation*}
                \mathbb E\left[\left(\eta(h)-\eta(h')\right)^2\right]
                =\left\lVertK_h-K_{h'}\right\rVert^2_{L^2(\nu)}.
            \end{equation*}
            Thus $\eta(h)=\eta(h')$ almost surely whenever $K_h=K_{h'}$ in
            $L^2(\nu)$, so $K_h\mapsto\eta(h)$ is a well-defined linear
            isometry on the subspace of functions $K_h$. This subspace is
            dense by Lemma~\ref{L: Kh_dense}, so the map extends uniquely
            by continuity to a linear isometry
            $W:L^2(\nu)\to L^2(\mathbb P)$. Since $K_1=\1$ and $\eta(1)=1$, we
            have $W\1=\1$.

            Being an isometry, $W$ is bounded with $\left\lVertW\right\rVert=1$. For each
            $u\in L^2(\mathbb P)$, the map $g\mapsto\left\langle u,Wg\right\rangle_{L^2(\mathbb P)}$ is
            therefore a bounded linear functional on $L^2(\nu)$, and the
            Riesz representation theorem gives a unique $W^*u\in L^2(\nu)$
            with
            \begin{equation*}
                \left\langle W^*u,g\right\rangle_{L^2(\nu)}=\left\langle u,Wg\right\rangle_{L^2(\mathbb P)},
                \quad g\in L^2(\nu).
            \end{equation*}
            This defines the adjoint $W^*:L^2(\mathbb P)\to L^2(\nu)$, a bounded
            linear operator with $\left\lVertW^*\right\rVert=\left\lVertW\right\rVert=1$. Since $W$
            preserves inner products, $W^*W=I$. By~\eqref{E: WKh} and the
            density of the functions $K_h$, $W^*u$ is the unique element of
            $L^2(\nu)$ satisfying~\eqref{E: adjoint_characterization} for
            every $h$.

            (b) The third moment identity implies the second, so (a)
            applies. Since $\eta(h)$ and
            $K_h$ are real-valued and bounded by $\left\lVerth\right\rVert_\infty$, the multiplication operators $M^\mathbb P_{\eta(h)}$ and
            $M^\nu_{K_h}$ are bounded and self-adjoint. Hence
            both sides of~\eqref{E: compressed_multiplication} are bounded
            operators on $L^2(\nu)$. Integrating $h'\otimes h\otimes h''$
            against both sides of the third moment identity, and using the
            definition of $W^*$ and~\eqref{E: WKh}, we obtain
            \begin{align*}
                \left\langle K_{h'},W^*M^\mathbb P_{\eta(h)}WK_{h''}\right\rangle_{L^2(\nu)}
                &=\left\langle WK_{h'},M^\mathbb P_{\eta(h)}WK_{h''}\right\rangle_{L^2(\mathbb P)}
                =\mathbb E[\eta(h')\eta(h)\eta(h'')]\\
                &=\int_YK_{h'}K_hK_{h''}\,d\nu
                =\left\langle K_{h'},M^\nu_{K_h}K_{h''}\right\rangle_{L^2(\nu)}.
            \end{align*}
            Thus the bounded bilinear forms
            $(f,g)\mapsto\left\langle f,W^*M^\mathbb P_{\eta(h)}Wg\right\rangle$ and
            $(f,g)\mapsto\left\langle f,M^\nu_{K_h}g\right\rangle$ on $L^2(\nu)$ agree whenever
            both arguments lie in the dense subspace of functions $K_h$.
            By continuity they agree everywhere, which
            proves~\eqref{E: compressed_multiplication}.

            (c) The fourth moment identity implies the second and third, so
            (a) and (b) apply. Abbreviate $M:=M^\mathbb P_{\eta(h)}$ and
            $N:=M^\nu_{K_h}$. Integrating $h'\otimes h\otimes h\otimes h''$
            against both sides of the fourth moment identity gives, as
            in~(b),
            \begin{align*}
                \left\langle K_{h'},W^*M^2WK_{h''}\right\rangle_{L^2(\nu)}
                &=\left\langle WK_{h'},M^2WK_{h''}\right\rangle_{L^2(\mathbb P)}
                =\mathbb E[\eta(h')\eta(h)^2\eta(h'')]\\
                &=\int_YK_{h'}K_h^2K_{h''}\,d\nu
                =\left\langle K_{h'},N^2K_{h''}\right\rangle_{L^2(\nu)},
            \end{align*}
            and the density argument of~(b) yields
            \begin{equation*}
                W^*M^2W=N^2.
            \end{equation*}
            For $g\in L^2(\nu)$, self-adjointness of $M$ and $N$, the
            definition of $W^*$, the preceding identities, and the isometry
            property of $W$ give the following calculation, with inner
            products in $L^2(\mathbb P)$ on the first line and in $L^2(\nu)$
            thereafter:
            \begin{align*}
                \left\lVertMWg-WNg\right\rVert^2_{L^2(\mathbb P)}
                &=\left\langle Wg,M^2Wg\right\rangle-2\left\langle Wg,MW(Ng)\right\rangle+\left\lVertW(Ng)\right\rVert^2\\
                &=\left\langle g,W^*M^2Wg\right\rangle-2\left\langle g,W^*MW(Ng)\right\rangle+\left\lVertNg\right\rVert^2\\
                &=\left\langle g,N^2g\right\rangle-2\left\langle g,N^2g\right\rangle+\left\lVertNg\right\rVert^2\\
                &=\left\lVertNg\right\rVert^2-2\left\lVertNg\right\rVert^2+\left\lVertNg\right\rVert^2=0.
            \end{align*}
            Since $g$ was arbitrary, $MW=WN$, which
            is~\eqref{E: exact_intertwining}.

label: R: finite_surjectivity
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{R: finite_surjectivity}
            Suppose the target has $m$ linearly independent components
            and the competing directing law has at most $m$ atoms.
            Realize the competitor canonically on its finite support.
            The isometry in Lemma~\ref{L: moment_isometry}(a) then maps
            an $m$-dimensional space into a space of dimension at most
            $m$, so it is onto. Hence $WW^*=I$, and multiplying
            \eqref{E: compressed_multiplication} on the left by $W$
            gives exact intertwining from three observations. See
            Appendix~\ref{A: finite_mixture_operators} for the
            identification argument and its block-observation extension.

label: L: point_realization
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{L: point_realization}
            Let $W:L^2(\nu)\to L^2(\mathbb P)$ be a linear isometry with
            $W\1=\1$, and suppose that $W\1_B$ is an indicator for every
            $B$ in a $\pi$-system generating $\mathcal{B}(Y)$. Then there is a
            $Y$-valued random variable $A$ with law $\nu$ such that
            \begin{equation}\label{E: evaluation_isometry}
                Wg=g(A)\quad\text{in }L^2(\mathbb P)
            \end{equation}
            for every $g\in L^2(\nu)$.
            If, in addition, $W$ is the isometry of
            Lemma~\ref{L: moment_isometry}(a), then $\eta=P_A$ almost
            surely.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We first show that $W\1_B$ is an indicator function for any $B \in \mathcal{B}(Y)$.
            Since $W$ is a linear isometry, it preserves the inner product
            \begin{equation*}
                \mathbb E[Wf\,Wg]=\int_Y fg\,d\nu
            \end{equation*}
            for all $f, g \in L^2(\nu)$.
            Let $\mathcal{H}$ be the class of Borel sets $B\subseteq Y$ for
            which $W\1_B$ has an indicator version. This class contains
            $Y$ and is closed under complements because $W\1=\1$ and
            $W\1_{Y\setminus B}=\1-W\1_B$. If
            $B_1,B_2,\ldots\in\mathcal{H}$ are pairwise disjoint, choose
            indicator versions $S_j$ of $W\1_{B_j}$. For $i\neq j$,
            \begin{equation*}
                \mathbb E[S_iS_j]=\nu(B_i\cap B_j)=0.
            \end{equation*}
            Thus, outside a single null set, at most one $S_j$ equals
            one. The partial sums $\sum_{j\leq n}S_j$ therefore
            converge boundedly to an indicator, while
            $\sum_{j\leq n}\1_{B_j}\to\1_{\bigcup_jB_j}$ in
            $L^2(\nu)$. Continuity of $W$ and bounded convergence give
            \begin{equation*}
                W\1_{\bigcup_jB_j}=\sum_{j\geq1}S_j
                \quad\text{in }L^2(\mathbb P).
            \end{equation*}
            Hence $\mathcal{H}$ is a Dynkin system. It contains the generating
            $\pi$-system in the hypothesis, so the $\pi$-$\lambda$
            theorem gives $\mathcal{H}=\mathcal{B}(Y)$.
        
            We now construct the random parameter $A$. Since $Y$ is Polish,
            \cite[Theorem~1.8(ii)]{KallenbergFoundations} provides a Borel
            set $F\subseteq[0,1]$ and a bijection $\iota:Y\to F$ such
            that both $\iota$ and $\iota^{-1}$ are Borel measurable.
            For $q\in\mathbb Q$, put
            \begin{equation*}
                B_q:=\{y\in Y:\iota(y)>q\},
            \end{equation*}
            and choose an indicator version $S_q$ of $W\1_{B_q}$.
            Since $W\1=\1$, the inner-product identity gives
            $\mathbb E[S_q]=\nu(B_q)$. For rational $q<r$,
            \begin{equation*}
                \mathbb E[S_r(1-S_q)]
                =\nu(B_r)-\nu(B_r\cap B_q)=0,
            \end{equation*}
            so $S_r\leq S_q$ almost surely. Moreover, $S_q=1$ for $q<0$
            and $S_q=0$ for $q\geq1$, almost surely. These relations
            hold simultaneously outside a common measurable null set.
            On that null set, replace $S_q$ by $\1_{\{q<0\}}$,
            so the relations hold everywhere. Define
            \begin{equation*}
                R:=\sup\{q\in\mathbb Q:S_q=1\}\in[0,1].
            \end{equation*}
            For each rational $q$, nesting gives
            \begin{equation*}
                \{R>q\}
                =\bigcup_{n\geq1}\{S_{q+1/n}=1\}
                \subseteq\{S_q=1\}.
            \end{equation*}
            In particular, $R$ is measurable. Since
            $B_{q+1/n}\uparrow B_q$, continuity from below gives
            \begin{equation*}
                \mathbb P(R>q)
                =\lim_{n\to\infty}\mathbb E[S_{q+1/n}]
                =\lim_{n\to\infty}\nu(B_{q+1/n})
                =\nu(B_q)
                =\mathbb E[S_q].
            \end{equation*}
            Consequently, $S_q=\1_{\{R>q\}}$ almost surely, and $R$
            has law $\iota_*\nu$. In particular, $R\in F$ almost
            surely. Fix $y_0\in Y$ and define
            \begin{equation*}
                A:=
                \begin{cases}
                    \iota^{-1}(R),& R\in F,\\
                    y_0,& R\notin F.
                \end{cases}
            \end{equation*}
            Because $F$ is Borel and $\iota^{-1}$ is measurable,
            $A$ is measurable, and its law is $\nu$.
        
            We now identify $W$ with evaluation at $A$. For every
            rational $q$,
            \begin{equation*}
                W\1_{B_q}=S_q
                =\1_{\{R>q\}}
                =\1_{\{A\in B_q\}}
                \quad\text{almost surely}.
            \end{equation*}
            Since $\iota$ is a Borel isomorphism, the sets $B_q$ form
            a $\pi$-system containing $Y$ and generating $\mathcal{B}(Y)$.
            Their indicators span a dense subspace of $L^2(\nu)$:
            the Borel sets whose indicators lie in the closed linear
            span form a Dynkin system containing this $\pi$-system,
            so the span contains all Borel indicators.
            Evaluation $g\mapsto g(A)$ is an isometry because $A$
            has law $\nu$. Its agreement with $W$ on a dense
            subspace therefore proves \eqref{E: evaluation_isometry}.
        
            If $W$ is the isometry of
            Lemma~\ref{L: moment_isometry}(a), then
            \eqref{E: WKh} and \eqref{E: evaluation_isometry} give
            \begin{equation*}
                \eta(h)=WK_h=K_h(A)=P_A(h)
            \end{equation*}
            almost surely for each bounded Borel function $h$.
            Apply this to the indicators of a countable algebra
            generating $\mathcal{B}(E)$ and intersect the resulting
            probability-one events. Then $\eta$ and $P_A$ agree
            on that algebra, and hence on $\mathcal{B}(E)$, almost surely.

label: L: localization_completeness
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The first implication follows by integrating over
            $Y\setminus B$. For the second, let $\mathcal{A}$ be the countable
            generating $\pi$-system in~\eqref{E: weak_localization}.
            If $Q_\nu[f]=0$, then $\int_Y f\,d\nu=0$, and
            \eqref{E: weak_localization} gives
            $\int_{Y\setminus B}f\,d\nu=0$, hence $\int_B f\,d\nu=0$,
            for every $B\in\mathcal{A}$. Since $\mathcal{A}\cup\{Y\}$ is a generating
            $\pi$-system, uniqueness of finite signed measures gives
            $f\,d\nu=0$. Thus $f=0$ $\nu$-almost everywhere.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $\eta$ be a random probability measure on $E$, defined on
            $(\Omega,\Sigma,\mathbb P)$, satisfying~\eqref{E: three_rigidity}. We need to show that $\eta = P_A$ almost surely for $A \sim \nu$. Weak
            localization implies completeness by
            Lemma~\ref{L: localization_completeness}, so
            Lemma~\ref{L: moment_isometry}(a,b) applies and provides the
            isometry $W$. By Lemma~\ref{L: point_realization}, it suffices
            to show that $S:=W\1_B$ is an indicator for every $B$ in the
            $\pi$-system $\mathcal{A}$ of~\eqref{E: weak_localization}. Fix such a
            $B$, and choose a finite measurable representative of $S=W\1_B$.

            If $\eta$ were already of the form $P_A$ for a $Y$-valued
            random variable $A$ with law $\nu$, then $W$ would be
            evaluation at $A$, by the uniqueness in
            Lemma~\ref{L: moment_isometry}(a), since evaluation at $A$ is
            an isometry sending $K_h$ to $K_h(A)=\eta(h)$. In that case
            $S=\1_{\{A\in B\}}$. For general $\eta$, we use that $S$ is an
            indicator exactly when $S^2(1-S)=0$ almost surely. It
            therefore suffices to prove that
            \begin{equation}\label{E: cubic_identity}
                \mathbb E[\1_DS^2(1-S)]=0
            \end{equation}
            for every event $D\in\Sigma$ on which $S$ is bounded. Indeed,
            put $H:=S^2(1-S)$ and fix $N\geq1$. For
            $D=\{\left|S\right|\leq N,\ H>0\}$,~\eqref{E: cubic_identity} gives
            $\mathbb E[\1_DH]=0$ with $H>0$ on $D$, so $\mathbb P(D)=0$. The same
            argument applies to $\{\left|S\right|\leq N,\ H<0\}$. Thus $H=0$
            almost surely on $\{\left|S\right|\leq N\}$. Since these events
            increase to $\Omega$, letting $N\to\infty$ gives $H=0$ almost
            surely.

            To prove~\eqref{E: cubic_identity}, fix $D\in\Sigma$ on which
            $S$ is bounded, and consider the localized measure $\mu_D$ on $E$ defined by
            \begin{equation*}
                \mu_D(C):=\mathbb E[\1_DS^2\eta(C)]
            \end{equation*}
            for all $C \in\mathcal{B}(E)$, i.e. $\eta$ averaged over $D$ with weight $S^2$. Since
            $0\leq\eta(C)\leq1$ and $S\in L^2(\mathbb P)$, monotone convergence
            shows that $\mu_D$ is a finite positive measure, and
            $\mu_D(h)=\mathbb E[\1_DS^2\eta(h)]$ for every bounded Borel $h$. The
            same holds for the unlocalized measure $\mu_\Omega$. Because
            $S$ is bounded on $D$, the random variable $\1_DS^2$ is bounded
            and so lies in $L^2(\mathbb P)$. Put
            \begin{equation*}
                f_D:=W^*(\1_DS^2)\in L^2(\nu).
            \end{equation*}
            We show that, in the setwise order on measures,
            \begin{equation}\label{E: localized_sandwich}
                0\leq Q_\nu[f_D]=\mu_D\leq\mu_\Omega=Q_\nu[\1_B].
            \end{equation}
            The first equality says that $\mu_D$ is a mixture of the
            components with signed weight $f_D$. The last says that the
            unlocalized measure is the mixture of the components with
            parameters in $B$. The inequalities are immediate, and
            together these facts place $f_D$ within the scope of weak
            localization.

            For the first equality,~\eqref{E: adjoint_characterization}
            with $u=\1_DS^2$ gives, for every bounded Borel $h$,
            \begin{equation*}
                \mu_D(h)
                =\mathbb E[\1_DS^2\eta(h)]
                =\left\langle f_D,K_h\right\rangle_{L^2(\nu)}
                =\int_Yf_D(y)P_y(h)\,d\nu(y)
                =Q_\nu[f_D](h).
            \end{equation*}
            The inequalities $0\leq\mu_D\leq\mu_\Omega$ hold because
            $0\leq\1_DS^2\leq S^2$ and $\eta\geq0$. For the last equality,
            the compression
            identity~\eqref{E: compressed_multiplication} gives, for every
            bounded Borel $h$,
            \begin{align*}
                \mu_\Omega(h)
                &=\left\langle W\1_B,M^\mathbb P_{\eta(h)}W\1_B\right\rangle_{L^2(\mathbb P)}
                =\left\langle \1_B,W^*M^\mathbb P_{\eta(h)}W\1_B\right\rangle_{L^2(\nu)}\\
                &=\left\langle \1_B,M^\nu_{K_h}\1_B\right\rangle_{L^2(\nu)}
                =\int_BP_y(h)\,d\nu(y)
                =Q_\nu[\1_B](h).
            \end{align*}

            By~\eqref{E: localized_sandwich}, weak localization applies to
            $f_D$. By weak localization, the definition of $W^*$, and
            $W(\1-\1_B)=\1-S$, we obtain
            \begin{align*}
                0
                &=\int_{Y\setminus B}f_D\,d\nu\\
                &=\left\langle W^*(\1_DS^2),\1-\1_B\right\rangle_{L^2(\nu)}\\
                &=\left\langle \1_DS^2,W(\1-\1_B)\right\rangle_{L^2(\mathbb P)}\\
                &=\mathbb E[\1_DS^2(1-S)].
            \end{align*}
            This proves~\eqref{E: cubic_identity}.

            Hence $W\1_B$ is an indicator for every $B\in\mathcal{A}$.
            Lemma~\ref{L: point_realization} now gives a $Y$-valued random
            variable $A$ with law $\nu$ such that $\eta=P_A$ almost surely,
            so $\mathcal{L}(\eta)=\mathfrak{G}_\nu$.

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $\eta$ be a random probability measure on $E$, defined on
            $(\Omega,\Sigma,\mathbb P)$, with
            $\mathbb E[\eta^{\otimes4}]=\mathcal{M}_4(\mathfrak{G}_\nu)$. We need to show that $\eta = P_A$ almost surely for $A \sim \nu$. Since $(\nu,P)$
            satisfies~\eqref{E: completeness},
            Lemma~\ref{L: moment_isometry}(a,c) supplies an isometry $W$
            satisfying the exact intertwining
            identity~\eqref{E: exact_intertwining}. By
            Lemma~\ref{L: point_realization}, it suffices to show that
            $W\1_B$ is an indicator for every Borel set $B$.
        
            Fix such a $B$ and put $S:=W\1_B$. By
            Lemma~\ref{L: Kh_dense}, we may choose bounded Borel maps
            $h_n:E\to\mathbb R$ such that $K_{h_n}\to\1_B$ in $L^2(\nu)$.
            Applying~\eqref{E: exact_intertwining} to $\1_B$ gives
            \begin{equation*}
                W(K_{h_n}\1_B)=\eta(h_n)S.
            \end{equation*}
            Since $W$ is an isometry and $\mathbb P$ is a probability measure,
            \begin{align*}
                \left\lVertW(K_{h_n}\1_B)-S\right\rVert_{L^1(\mathbb P)}
                &\leq\left\lVertW(K_{h_n}\1_B)-W\1_B\right\rVert_{L^2(\mathbb P)}\\
                &=\left\lVert(K_{h_n}-\1_B)\1_B\right\rVert_{L^2(\nu)}\\
                &\leq\left\lVertK_{h_n}-\1_B\right\rVert_{L^2(\nu)}
                \longrightarrow0.
            \end{align*}
            On the other hand, $\eta(h_n)=WK_{h_n}$, so the
            Cauchy--Schwarz inequality gives
            \begin{align*}
                \left\lVert\eta(h_n)S-S^2\right\rVert_{L^1(\mathbb P)}
                &\leq\left\lVert\eta(h_n)-S\right\rVert_{L^2(\mathbb P)}
                     \left\lVertS\right\rVert_{L^2(\mathbb P)}\\
                &=\left\lVertK_{h_n}-\1_B\right\rVert_{L^2(\nu)}
                     \left\lVertS\right\rVert_{L^2(\mathbb P)}
                \longrightarrow0.
            \end{align*}
            The intertwining identity identifies the two sequences,
            so uniqueness of the $L^1(\mathbb P)$ limit gives $S=S^2$
            almost surely. Thus $W\1_B$ is an indicator for every
            Borel set $B$. Lemma~\ref{L: point_realization} yields
            a $Y$-valued random variable $A$ with law $\nu$ such that
            $\eta=P_A$ almost surely, and hence
            $\mathcal{L}(\eta)=\mathfrak{G}_\nu$.

label: C: translation_gaussian_rigidity
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{C: translation_gaussian_rigidity}
            Let $g\in\mathcal{P}(\mathbb R^p)$ have a characteristic function whose zero
            set has empty interior, and let $P_y=g(\,\cdot-y)$.
            Then $\mathfrak{G}_\nu$ is $4$-rigid for every $\nu\in\mathcal{P}(\mathbb R^p)$.
            In particular, if the first four coordinates of an infinite
            exchangeable sequence are jointly Gaussian, then the sequence
            is a Gaussian process.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
For Borel $B\subseteq\mathbb R^p$, the map
            $y\mapsto P_y(B)=\int_{\mathbb R^p}\1_B(y+z)\,g(dz)$ is Borel by
            Tonelli's theorem, so $P$ is a measurable probability kernel.
            Fix $\nu\in\mathcal{P}(\mathbb R^p)$ and a real $f\in L^2(\nu)\subseteq L^1(\nu)$,
            and put $\sigma:=f\nu$. For a finite signed measure $\tau$ on
            $\mathbb R^p$, write $\widehat\tau(t):=\int e^{i\left\langle t,x\right\rangle}\,\tau(dx)$.
            By Fubini's theorem, $Q_\nu[f]=\sigma*g$, and hence
            \begin{equation*}
                \widehat{Q_\nu[f]}(t)=\widehat\sigma(t)\,\widehat g(t),
                \quad t\in\mathbb R^p.
            \end{equation*}
            If $Q_\nu[f]=0$, then the continuous function $\widehat\sigma$
            vanishes on $\{\widehat g\neq0\}$, which is dense by hypothesis,
            and therefore everywhere. Uniqueness of Fourier transforms of
            finite signed measures gives $\sigma=0$, that is, $f=0$
            $\nu$-almost everywhere. Thus \eqref{E: completeness} holds, and
            Theorem~\ref{T: completeness_rigidity} shows that $\mathfrak{G}_\nu$ is
            $4$-rigid.

            For the Gaussian assertion, let $X$ be an infinite exchangeable sequence with
            $(X_1,\ldots,X_4)$ jointly Gaussian, and put $\mu:=\mathbb E X_1$,
            $b:=\operatorname{Cov}(X_1,X_2)$, and
            $a:=\operatorname{Var}(X_1)-b$. By exchangeability,
            $2a=\operatorname{Var}(X_1-X_2)\geq0$ and
            \begin{equation*}
                0\leq\operatorname{Var}\Bigl(\frac1n\sum_{j=1}^nX_j\Bigr)
                =\frac an+b
                \quad\text{for all }n\geq1,
            \end{equation*}
            so $b\geq0$. With the convention $\mathcal N(m,0):=\delta_m$,
            apply the first part with $g=\mathcal N(0,a)$, whose
            characteristic function $e^{-at^2/2}$ never vanishes, and
            $\nu=\mathcal N(\mu,b)$; let $\Gamma$ be the resulting
            $4$-rigid directing law. If $A\sim\mathcal N(\mu,b)$ is
            independent of iid standard Gaussian variables
            $G_1,G_2,\ldots$, then $Y_j:=A+\sqrt a\,G_j$ are conditionally
            iid with law $\mathcal N(A,a)$, so
            $\mathcal{L}(Y_1,\ldots,Y_n)=\mathcal{M}_n(\Gamma)$ for every $n$. Each such
            block is Gaussian with mean $\mu$ in every coordinate and
            covariance matrix $aI+bJ$, where $J$ is the all-ones matrix.
            The block $(X_1,\ldots,X_4)$ has the same mean and covariance,
            so the directing law $\Lambda$ of $X$ satisfies
            $\mathcal{M}_4(\Lambda)=\mathcal{L}(X_1,\ldots,X_4)=\mathcal{M}_4(\Gamma)$. Hence
            $\Lambda=\Gamma$, and every finite block of $X$ has the
            Gaussian law $\mathcal{M}_n(\Gamma)=\mathcal{L}(Y_1,\ldots,Y_n)$. Thus $X$ is a
            Gaussian process.

label: Ex: uniform_localization
title: Example
body_md:
\label{Ex: uniform_localization}
            Let $E=Y=(0,\infty)$ and let $P_y$ be the uniform
            probability measure on $(0,y)$. For every
            $\nu\in\mathcal{P}(Y)$, the pair $(\nu,P)$ satisfies strong
            localization, and hence $\mathfrak{G}_\nu$ is $3$-rigid.
        
            To see this, take the countable generating $\pi$-system
            \begin{equation*}
                \mathcal{A}=\{Y\}\cup
                \{(0,b]:b\in\mathbb Q,\ b>0\}.
            \end{equation*}
            For real $f\in L^2(\nu)$, the signed mixture $Q_\nu[f]$
            has Lebesgue density
            \begin{equation*}
                q_f(x):=\int_{(x,\infty)}\frac{f(y)}{y}\,d\nu(y),
                \quad x>0.
            \end{equation*}
            This integral is absolutely convergent for every $x>0$,
            and $q_f$ is right-continuous. If $B=(0,b]$ and
            \begin{equation*}
                0\leq Q_\nu[f]\leq Q_\nu[\mathbf1_B],
            \end{equation*}
            then $q_f(x)=0$ for Lebesgue-almost every $x>b$,
            since $Q_\nu[\mathbf1_B]$ is supported on $(0,b]$.
            Right-continuity gives $q_f(x)=0$ for every $x>b$.
            Therefore
            \begin{equation*}
                \int_{(a,c]}\frac{f(y)}{y}\,d\nu(y)
                =q_f(a)-q_f(c)=0,
                \quad b<a<c<\infty.
            \end{equation*}
            Uniqueness of finite signed measures on $(b,\infty)$
            now gives $f=0$ $\nu$-almost everywhere on $(b,\infty)$,
            proving \eqref{E: strong_localization}.

title: Proof
body_md:
We prove the cycle (i)$\Rightarrow$(iii)$\Rightarrow$(ii)$\Rightarrow$(i).
            The first implication uses the Arendt--Batty--Hieber--Neubrander
            support theorem for Laplace transforms sampled along a M\"untz
            sequence; the last uses the full M\"untz theorem to construct a
            measure contradicting (ii).

            Assume (i), fix $\sigma\ne0$, and set
            $\delta:=\inf_{n\geq0}(\lambda_{n+1}-\lambda_n)>0$.
            Replacing $\lambda_n$ by $\frac{\lambda_n}{\delta}$ and $\sigma$
            by its image under $y\mapsto\delta y$ multiplies both sides of
            (iii) by $\delta$ and leaves (i) unchanged. For the proof of
            this implication, we may therefore assume
            $\lambda_{n+1}-\lambda_n\geq1$ for all $n\geq0$, so $\lambda_n\geq n$.

            Since $(\lambda_n)_{n\geq1}$ has gaps at least one and divergent
            reciprocal sum, parts (i) and (ii) of
            \cite[Theorem~2.8.3, p.~103]{ArendtEtAl2011}
            together give
            \begin{equation*}
                \inf\operatorname{supp}\left(|H(t)|\,dt\right)
                =-\limsup_{n\to\infty}\frac{1}{\lambda_n}
                    \log\left|\int_0^\infty e^{-\lambda_n t}H(t)\,dt\right|
            \end{equation*}
            for every bounded measurable function $H$ on $[0,\infty)$
            that is not zero almost everywhere.
            Put $F(t):=\sigma([0,t])$, a bounded right-continuous function.
            For every $b>0$, $F=0$ almost everywhere on $[0,b)$ if and only
            if $\sigma|_{[0,b)}=0$. Indeed, right-continuity turns
            almost-everywhere vanishing into pointwise vanishing on $[0,b)$,
            and
            $\sigma(\{0\})=F(0)$ and $\sigma((s,t])=F(t)-F(s)$ determine
            the restriction of $\sigma$ to $[0,b)$. Consequently,
            \begin{equation*}
                \inf\operatorname{supp}\left(|F(t)|\,dt\right)=\inf\operatorname{supp}|\sigma|.
            \end{equation*}
            Each side is the supremum of the $b\geq0$ for which the
            corresponding measure vanishes on $[0,b)$.
            Since $\sigma\ne0$, letting $b\to\infty$ shows that $F$ is not
            zero almost everywhere, as the support theorem requires.

            For $\lambda>0$, the bound
            \begin{equation*}
                \int_{[0,\infty)}\int_y^\infty
                    e^{-\lambda t}\,dt\,d|\sigma|(y)
                \leq\frac{\|\sigma\|_{\mathrm{TV}}}{\lambda}<\infty
            \end{equation*}
            justifies Fubini's theorem, which gives
            \begin{equation*}
                \int_0^\infty e^{-\lambda t}F(t)\,dt
                =\int_{[0,\infty)}\int_y^\infty
                    e^{-\lambda t}\,dt\,d\sigma(y)
                =\frac{\widehat\sigma(\lambda)}{\lambda}.
            \end{equation*}
            We obtain
            \begin{align*}
                \inf\operatorname{supp}|\sigma|
                    &=-\limsup_{n\to\infty}\frac{1}{\lambda_n}
                        \log\left|\frac{\widehat\sigma(\lambda_n)}{\lambda_n}\right|\\
                    &=-\limsup_{n\to\infty}\frac{1}{\lambda_n}
                        \log|\widehat\sigma(\lambda_n)|.
            \end{align*}
            The first equality is the support identity applied to $F$.
            The second follows from
            \begin{equation*}
                \frac{1}{\lambda_n}
                    \log\left|\frac{\widehat\sigma(\lambda_n)}{\lambda_n}\right|
                =\frac{1}{\lambda_n}\log|\widehat\sigma(\lambda_n)|
                    -\frac{\log\lambda_n}{\lambda_n}.
            \end{equation*}
            Both sides of this identity are $-\infty$ when
            $\widehat\sigma(\lambda_n)=0$. Since $\lambda_n\geq n\to\infty$
            and $\frac{\log x}{x}\to0$ as $x\to\infty$, the correction
            tends to zero and does not affect the limsup.
            This proves (i)$\Rightarrow$(iii).

            Suppose (iii) holds, and fix a finite signed measure $\sigma$
            and $b\geq0$. The condition
            $\sigma|_{[0,b)}=0$ gives
            \begin{equation*}
                |\widehat\sigma(\lambda_n)|
                \leq\|\sigma\|_{\mathrm{TV}}e^{-b\lambda_n}
                \quad\text{ for all }\quad n\geq1,
            \end{equation*}
            proving the implication $\Rightarrow$ in \eqref{E: laplace_support}.
            If $\sigma=0$, the equivalence is immediate. If $\sigma\ne0$
            and the right-hand side of \eqref{E: laplace_support} holds,
            then $|\widehat\sigma(\lambda_n)|\leq Ce^{-b\lambda_n}$ for some
            $C>0$ and all $n\geq1$. Then
            \begin{equation*}
                \frac{1}{\lambda_n}\log|\widehat\sigma(\lambda_n)|
                \leq\frac{\log C}{\lambda_n}-b.
            \end{equation*}
            The gap condition implies $\lambda_n\to\infty$, so the limsup
            of the left-hand side is at most $-b$. By (iii),
            $\inf\operatorname{supp}|\sigma|\geq b$, and hence $\sigma|_{[0,b)}=0$.
            This proves (iii)$\Rightarrow$(ii).

            We prove (ii)$\Rightarrow$(i) by contraposition.
            Suppose $\sum_{n\geq1}\frac{1}{\lambda_n}<\infty$.
            Since $\frac{\lambda_n}{1+\lambda_n^2}\leq\frac{1}{\lambda_n}$,
            the full M\"untz theorem \cite[Theorem~2.1]{BorweinErdelyi1996}
            shows that $\operatorname{span}\{1,u^{\lambda_n}:n\geq1\}$
            is not dense in $C([0,1])$. The Hahn--Banach and Riesz
            representation theorems therefore give a nonzero finite real
            signed measure $\tau$ on $[0,1]$ such that
            \begin{equation*}
                \tau([0,1])=0
                \quad\text{and}\quad
                \int_{[0,1]}u^{\lambda_n}\,d\tau(u)=0
                \quad\text{ for all }\quad n\geq1.
            \end{equation*}
            The restriction $\tau|_{(0,1]}$ is nonzero, since otherwise
            the total-mass identity would force $\tau=0$. Let $\sigma$ be
            its image under $u\mapsto-\log u$. This map is a bijection from
            $(0,1]$ onto $[0,\infty)$ with inverse $y\mapsto e^{-y}$, so
            $\sigma\ne0$. For all $n\geq1$,
            \begin{equation*}
                \widehat\sigma(\lambda_n)
                =\int_{(0,1]}u^{\lambda_n}\,d\tau(u)
                =\int_{[0,1]}u^{\lambda_n}\,d\tau(u)=0,
            \end{equation*}
            where the second equality uses $\lambda_n>0$, so that
            $u^{\lambda_n}$ vanishes at $u=0$.
            The lower endpoint of $\operatorname{supp}|\sigma|$ is finite, so choose
            $b>\inf\operatorname{supp}|\sigma|$.
            The right-hand side of \eqref{E: laplace_support} holds trivially,
            but $\sigma|_{[0,b)}\ne0$. Thus (ii) fails, proving
            (ii)$\Rightarrow$(i).

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $\tau$ be the image of $\sigma$ under
            $y\mapsto(e^{-y_1},\ldots,e^{-y_d})$, regarded as a finite
            signed measure on $[0,1]^d$ with no mass outside $(0,1]^d$.
            The hypothesis says that every generalized product moment
            of $\tau$ is zero. By the full M\"untz theorem
            \cite[Theorem~2.1]{BorweinErdelyi1996}, the
            span of $\{u^{\lambda_{i,n}}:n\geq0\}$ is uniformly dense
            in $C([0,1])$ for each $i$: because
            $\lambda_{i,n}\to\infty$, the divergence of
            $\sum_n\frac{1}{\lambda_{i,n}}$ is equivalent to the
            divergence of
            $\sum_n\frac{\lambda_{i,n}}{1+\lambda_{i,n}^2}$.
            Approximating each factor of an ordinary monomial and
            using polynomial density on $[0,1]^d$ shows that the span
            of the generalized products is uniformly dense there. Integration against $\tau$ therefore
            vanishes on every continuous function. Hence $\tau=0$,
            and therefore $\sigma=0$.

title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{L: transform_continuity}
            For every $f\in L^2(\nu)$, the map $\mathcal L_\nu f$
            defined in \eqref{E: exponential_transform} is well-defined

head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Since $\nu$ is a probability measure, $f\in L^1(\nu)$.
            Fix $t\in U$ and choose $c$ with $t_0<c<t$.
            Lemma~\ref{L: normalizer_bound} gives a constant
            $C_c<\infty$ such that
            \begin{equation*}
                z(y)e^{-\langle y,c\rangle}\leq C_c,
                \quad y\in Y.
            \end{equation*}
            This proves that the integral in
            Equation~\eqref{E: exponential_transform} is absolutely
            convergent. If $t_n\to t$, then $t_n\geq c$ for all
            sufficiently large $n$, and hence
            \begin{equation*}
                \left|f(y)z(y)e^{-\langle y,t_n\rangle}\right|
                \leq C_c|f(y)|.
            \end{equation*}
            Dominated convergence then yields continuity at $t$.

title: Proof
body_md:
Fix $\nu\in\mathcal{P}(Y)$. We prove strong localization
            \eqref{E: strong_localization} for the countable generating
            $\pi$-system
            \begin{equation*}
                \mathcal{A}:=\left\{
                    B_b:=Y\cap\prod_{i=1}^d[b_i,\infty):
                    b\in(\mathbb Q\cap[0,\infty))^d
                \right\}.
            \end{equation*}
            Fix $B=B_b\in\mathcal{A}$ and a real $f\in L^2(\nu)$ satisfying
            \begin{equation*}
                0\leq Q_\nu[f]\leq Q_\nu[\1_B].
            \end{equation*}
            We must show that $f=0$ $\nu$-almost everywhere on $Y\setminus B$.
            We obtain bounds for a tilted signed measure and apply
            Lemma~\ref{L: multivariate_laplace_support} to exclude that set.
        
            By~\eqref{E: exponential_fubini}, the two signed mixtures have
            $m$-densities $(\mathcal L_\nu f)(T(\cdot))$ and
            $(\mathcal L_\nu\1_B)(T(\cdot))$. Since $\rho=T_*m$,
            their domination gives
            $0\leq\mathcal L_\nu f\leq\mathcal L_\nu\1_B$
            $\rho$-almost everywhere. The functions $\mathcal L_\nu f$ and
            $\mathcal L_\nu\1_B$ are continuous on $U$ by
            Lemma~\ref{L: transform_continuity}. Failure of either inequality
            at a point of $\operatorname{supp}\rho\cap U$ would therefore imply failure
            on an open neighborhood of positive $\rho$-measure. Consequently,
            \begin{equation*}
                0\leq(\mathcal L_\nu f)(t)
                    \leq(\mathcal L_\nu\1_B)(t)
                \quad
                \text{ for all }
                \quad t\in\operatorname{supp}\rho\cap U.
            \end{equation*}
        
            To use these inequalities at the points supplied
            by~\eqref{E: exponential_MS}, set
            \begin{align*}
                s&:=t_0+(\lambda_{1,1},\ldots,\lambda_{d,1}),\\
                \mu_{i,n}&:=\lambda_{i,n+1}-\lambda_{i,1}
                    \quad\text{ for all }\quad n\geq0,
            \end{align*}
            for each $1\leq i\leq d$.
            Each shifted sequence starts at zero and is uniformly separated.
            Its reciprocal sum diverges because
            $0<\mu_{i,n}<\lambda_{i,n+1}$ for every $n\geq1$.
            Writing $\mu_{\boldsymbol n}:=(\mu_{1,n_1},\ldots,\mu_{d,n_d})$,
            condition~\eqref{E: exponential_MS} gives
            $s+\mu_{\boldsymbol n}\in\operatorname{supp}\rho\cap U$ for every
            $\boldsymbol n\in\mathbb N_0^d$.
        
            Lemma~\ref{L: normalizer_bound}, applied with $c=s$, bounds
            $z(y)e^{-\left\langle y,s\right\rangle}$ on $Y$. Since $f\in L^1(\nu)$, the measure
            \begin{equation*}
                d\sigma_s(y):=f(y)z(y)e^{-\left\langle y,s\right\rangle}\,d\nu(y)
            \end{equation*}
            on $Y$, extended by zero outside $Y$, is finite. Moreover,
            \begin{equation*}
                C_s:=\int_B z(y)e^{-\left\langle y,s\right\rangle}\,d\nu(y)<\infty.
            \end{equation*}
            At $s+\mu_{\boldsymbol n}$, the transform inequalities give
            nonnegativity and the upper bound below. Since $y\geq b$ on $B$
            and $\mu_{\boldsymbol n}\geq0$, we obtain
            \begin{align}
                \left|\int_{[0,\infty)^d}
                    e^{-\left\langle y,\mu_{\boldsymbol n}\right\rangle}\,d\sigma_s(y)\right|
                &=(\mathcal L_\nu f)(s+\mu_{\boldsymbol n})\notag\\
                &\leq\int_B z(y)e^{-\left\langle y,s\right\rangle}
                    e^{-\left\langle y,\mu_{\boldsymbol n}\right\rangle}\,d\nu(y)\notag\\
                &\leq C_s e^{-\left\langle b,\mu_{\boldsymbol n}\right\rangle}
                    \label{E: exponential_transform_domination}
            \end{align}
            for every $\boldsymbol n\in\mathbb N_0^d$.
        
            Lemma~\ref{L: multivariate_laplace_support} now shows that
            $\sigma_s$ vanishes outside $\prod_{i=1}^d[b_i,\infty)$.
            Hence
            \begin{equation*}
                0=|\sigma_s|(Y\setminus B)
                =\int_{Y\setminus B}|f(y)|z(y)e^{-\left\langle y,s\right\rangle}\,d\nu(y).
            \end{equation*}
            The weight $z(y)e^{-\left\langle y,s\right\rangle}$ is strictly positive on $Y$,
            so $f=0$ $\nu$-almost everywhere on $Y\setminus B$.
            This proves strong localization. Strong localization implies
            weak localization, and Theorem~\ref{T: general_rigidity}
            therefore gives $3$-rigidity of $\mathfrak{G}_\nu$.

title: Proof
body_md:
We first verify the properties of the weight, then reduce
            completeness to injectivity on finite signed mixing measures.
            The substitution $u=e^{1-y}$ and a weighted translation
            relate injectivity to the weighted density condition.
            In the converse direction, the translation also supplies
            the possible missing zero at $t=a$.
        
            The integrand defining $w_\rho(u)$ is positive for $u>0$
            and bounded by $e^{-(t-a)}$, whose $\rho$-integral is
            $e^aZ(1)<\infty$. At zero it converges pointwise to
            $\mathbf1_{\{a\}}(t)$. Dominated convergence therefore
            gives continuity of $w_\rho$ on $[0,1]$, and positivity
            gives $w_\rho(u)>0$ on $(0,1]$.
        
            Set
            \begin{equation*}
                p_t(y):=\frac{e^{-ty}}{Z(y)}.
            \end{equation*}
            For $a<s<t$, we have
            $0<\rho([a,s])\leq e^sZ(1)<\infty$ and
            $Z(y)\geq e^{-sy}\rho([a,s])$. Hence
            \begin{equation*}
                0<p_t(y)\leq
                    \frac{e^{-(t-s)y}}{\rho([a,s])}
                \quad\text{ for all }\quad y>0.
            \end{equation*}
            Thus $p_t$ is bounded and tends to zero as $y\to\infty$.
            When $\rho(\{a\})>0$, we also have
            $p_a(y)\leq\frac{1}{\rho(\{a\})}$.
            The expression for $w_\rho$ gives
            \begin{equation}\label{E: exponential_completeness_substitution}
                p_{a+\lambda}(1-\log u)
                =e^{-\lambda}\frac{u^\lambda}{w_\rho(u)}
                \quad\text{ for all }\quad
                \lambda>0,\ u\in(0,1].
            \end{equation}
            Since $1-\log u\to\infty$ as $u\downarrow0$, this proves
            the asserted continuous extension of the weighted
            monomials at zero.
        
            Completeness for every mixing law is equivalent to
            injectivity of $\xi\mapsto\int P_y\,d\xi(y)$ on finite
            signed Borel measures on $(0,\infty)$. Indeed,
            injectivity applied to $d\xi=f\,d\nu$, with
            $f\in L^2(\nu)\subseteq L^1(\nu)$, gives completeness.
            Conversely, a nonzero $\xi$ in the kernel gives
            \begin{equation*}
                \nu:=\frac{|\xi|}{\left\lVert\xi\right\rVert_{\mathrm{TV}}},
                \quad
                f:=\frac{d\xi}{d|\xi|},
            \end{equation*}
            for which $|f|=1$ $\nu$-almost everywhere and
            $Q_\nu[f]=0$, so completeness fails.
        
            For such a signed measure $\xi$, define
            \begin{equation*}
                F_\xi(t):=\int_{(0,\infty)}p_t(y)\,d\xi(y),
                \quad t>a,
            \end{equation*}
            and also at $a$ when $\rho(\{a\})>0$.
            The preceding bounds make these integrals finite.
            Since $p_t\leq p_b$ whenever $t\geq b>a$, dominated
            convergence gives continuity of $F_\xi$ on $(a,\infty)$.
            Tonelli's theorem gives
            \begin{equation*}
                \int_{E\times(0,\infty)}p_{T(x)}(y)\,
                    d(m\otimes|\xi|)(x,y)
                =\left\lVert\xi\right\rVert_{\mathrm{TV}},
            \end{equation*}
            because each $P_y$ is a probability measure.
            Fubini's theorem therefore gives $F_\xi\circ T$ as the
            density of $\int P_y\,d\xi(y)$, with its value at $a$
            needed only when $\rho(\{a\})>0$. The signed mixture
            vanishes exactly when $F_\xi=0$ $\rho$-almost everywhere.
            Since $F_\xi$ is continuous on $(a,\infty)$, this is
            equivalent to
            \begin{equation}\label{E: exponential_completeness_kernel}
                F_\xi(t)=0
                \quad\text{ for all }\quad
                t\in\operatorname{supp}\rho\cap(a,\infty),
                \quad\text{ and }\quad
                F_\xi(a)=0\text{ if }\rho(\{a\})>0.
            \end{equation}
        
            We use $u=e^{1-y}$ so that
            $w_\rho(1)=e^aZ(1)$ is finite even when $\rho$ has
            infinite mass. To move arbitrary mixing measures into
            $(1,\infty)$, define
            \begin{equation*}
                \int h\,d(\tau\xi)
                :=\int h(y+1)e^a\frac{Z(y+1)}{Z(y)}\,d\xi(y)
            \end{equation*}
            for bounded Borel measurable $h$.
            Since $\rho$ is concentrated on $[a,\infty)$, the
            multiplier lies in $(0,1]$. Thus $\tau\xi$ is finite
            and concentrated on $(1,\infty)$; positivity of the
            multiplier and injectivity of translation also make
            $\tau$ injective. Direct substitution gives
            \begin{equation}\label{E: exponential_completeness_translation}
                F_{\tau\xi}(t)=e^{-(t-a)}F_\xi(t)
                \quad\text{ for all }\quad t>a,
            \end{equation}
            and also at $a$ when $\rho(\{a\})>0$.
        
            Put $C_0:=\{g\in C[0,1]:g(0)=0\}$, identified by
            restriction with $C_0((0,1])$.
            Suppose first that \eqref{E: weighted_muntz_completeness}
            holds and $\xi$ satisfies
            \eqref{E: exponential_completeness_kernel}.
            Let $\sigma$ be the pushforward of $\tau\xi$ under
            $y\mapsto e^{1-y}$, viewed as a measure on $(0,1]$.
            For every $\lambda\in\mathcal S_\rho$,
            \begin{equation*}
                \int_{(0,1]}\frac{u^\lambda}{w_\rho(u)}\,d\sigma(u)
                =e^\lambda F_{\tau\xi}(a+\lambda)
                =F_\xi(a+\lambda)=0,
            \end{equation*}
            since $a+\lambda\in\operatorname{supp}\rho\cap(a,\infty)$.
            Density implies that $\sigma$ annihilates $C_0$,
            so Riesz uniqueness gives $\sigma=0$.
            Hence $\tau\xi=0$, and injectivity of $\tau$ gives
            $\xi=0$.
        
            Conversely, if \eqref{E: weighted_muntz_completeness}
            fails, Hahn--Banach and Riesz representation on
            $C_0((0,1])$ give a nonzero finite signed measure
            $\sigma$ on $(0,1]$ annihilating every weighted monomial.
            Its pushforward $\xi$ under $u\mapsto1-\log u$ is
            nonzero, finite, and concentrated on $[1,\infty)$.
            By \eqref{E: exponential_completeness_substitution},
            $F_\xi(a+\lambda)=0$ for all
            $\lambda\in\mathcal S_\rho$.
            Set $\zeta:=\xi-\tau\xi$. Then
            \begin{equation*}
                F_\zeta(t)=\bigl(1-e^{-(t-a)}\bigr)F_\xi(t)
            \end{equation*}
            for $t>a$, and also at $a$ when $\rho(\{a\})>0$.
            Thus $\zeta$ satisfies
            \eqref{E: exponential_completeness_kernel}, including
            the possible condition at $a$.
            Moreover, $y_0:=\min\operatorname{supp}|\xi|\geq1$ exists, and
            $|\xi|([y_0,y_0+1))>0$. Since $\tau\xi$ is concentrated
            on $[y_0+1,\infty)$, $\zeta$ agrees with $\xi$ on this
            interval and is therefore nonzero. Injectivity fails.
        
            This proves the equivalence. The rigidity conclusion
            follows from Theorem~\ref{T: completeness_rigidity}.

title: Proof
body_md:
By Proposition~\ref{P: exponential_completeness}, it
            suffices to show that
            \eqref{E: weighted_muntz_completeness} is equivalent to
            the divergence condition in
            Corollary~\ref{C: exponential_completeness_atom}. We
            remove the weight using the atom at $a$, adjoin the
            constants to reach the setting of the full M\"untz
            theorem, and then reduce arbitrary exponent sets to
            countable ones. Let $C_0$ be as in the proof of
            Proposition~\ref{P: exponential_completeness}. For
            $\mathcal S\subseteq(0,\infty)$, write
            \begin{equation*}
                \mathcal V(\mathcal S)
                :=\operatorname{span}
                    \bigl(\{\mathbf1\}\cup\{u^\lambda:\lambda\in\mathcal S\}\bigr),
                \quad
                \Delta(\mathcal S)
                :=\sup_{\substack{F\subseteq\mathcal S\\F\text{ finite}}}
                    \sum_{\lambda\in F}\frac{\lambda}{1+\lambda^2}.
            \end{equation*}
            The full M\"untz theorem concerns density of
            $\mathcal V(\mathcal S)$, and the condition in
            Corollary~\ref{C: exponential_completeness_atom} reads
            $\Delta(\mathcal S_\rho)=\infty$.
         
            We first remove the weight. For $0<u\leq1$, the integrand
            defining $w_\rho(u)$ is nonnegative, equals $1$ at $t=a$,
            and is at most $e^{-(t-a)}$. Together with
            $w_\rho(0)=\rho(\{a\})$, this gives
            \begin{equation*}
                0<\rho(\{a\})\leq w_\rho(u)\leq e^aZ(1)<\infty
                \quad\text{ for all }\quad u\in[0,1].
            \end{equation*}
            By Proposition~\ref{P: exponential_completeness},
            $w_\rho$ is continuous, so $\frac{1}{w_\rho}$ is
            continuous and bounded as well. Multiplication by
            $w_\rho$ is therefore a linear homeomorphism of $C_0$
            onto itself, with inverse given by multiplication by
            $\frac{1}{w_\rho}$. It sends each weighted monomial
            $\frac{u^\lambda}{w_\rho(u)}$ to $u^\lambda$. Hence
            \eqref{E: weighted_muntz_completeness} holds if and only
            if $\operatorname{span}\{u^\lambda:\lambda\in\mathcal S_\rho\}$
            is dense in $C_0$.
         
            We next adjoin the constants. Let $V\subseteq C_0$ be a
            subspace. If $V$ is dense in $C_0$, the decomposition
            $g=g(0)+(g-g(0))$ shows that $\mathbb R\mathbf1+V$ is dense in
            $C[0,1]$. Conversely, the projection $g\mapsto g-g(0)$ is
            a continuous linear map of $C[0,1]$ onto $C_0$ that sends
            $\mathbb R\mathbf1+V$ onto $V$. It therefore carries density of
            $\mathbb R\mathbf1+V$ in $C[0,1]$ to density of $V$ in $C_0$.
            Applied to
            $V=\operatorname{span}\{u^\lambda:\lambda\in\mathcal S_\rho\}$,
            for which $\mathbb R\mathbf1+V=\mathcal V(\mathcal S_\rho)$,
            this shows that \eqref{E: weighted_muntz_completeness}
            holds if and only if $\mathcal V(\mathcal S_\rho)$ is
            dense in $C[0,1]$.
         
            We now apply the full M\"untz theorem. For countable
            $\mathcal S$, the summands are positive, so
            $\Delta(\mathcal S)$ is the sum of the series in any
            enumeration of $\mathcal S$. The full M\"untz theorem
            \cite[Theorem~2.1]{BorweinErdelyi1996} characterizes
            density for an arbitrary sequence of distinct positive
            exponents, with no separation or monotonicity condition.
            This generality is needed here, since $\mathcal S_\rho$
            may have finite accumulation points. For countably
            infinite $\mathcal S$, the theorem states that
            $\mathcal V(\mathcal S)$ is dense in $C[0,1]$ if and only
            if $\Delta(\mathcal S)=\infty$. The same equivalence holds
            for finite $\mathcal S$, including $\mathcal S=\emptyset$,
            since then $\Delta(\mathcal S)<\infty$ and
            $\mathcal V(\mathcal S)$ is finite-dimensional, hence
            closed and proper. Thus, for every countable
            $\mathcal S\subseteq(0,\infty)$, density of
            $\mathcal V(\mathcal S)$ in $C[0,1]$ is equivalent to
            $\Delta(\mathcal S)=\infty$.
         
            It remains to remove the countability assumption. If
            $\Delta(\mathcal S_\rho)=\infty$, choose finite sets
            $F_n\subseteq\mathcal S_\rho$ such that
            \begin{equation*}
                \sum_{\lambda\in F_n}\frac{\lambda}{1+\lambda^2}\geq n
                \quad\text{ for all }\quad n\geq1.
            \end{equation*}
            Their union $\mathcal S'$ is countable and satisfies
            $\Delta(\mathcal S')=\infty$. Hence
            $\mathcal V(\mathcal S')$ is dense, and so is the larger
            space $\mathcal V(\mathcal S_\rho)$. If
            $\Delta(\mathcal S_\rho)<\infty$, then for each $k\geq1$
            at most $k\Delta(\mathcal S_\rho)$ exponents satisfy
            $\frac{\lambda}{1+\lambda^2}\geq\frac{1}{k}$. Every
            $\lambda>0$ satisfies this inequality for some $k$, so
            $\mathcal S_\rho$ is countable. The countable case then
            shows that $\mathcal V(\mathcal S_\rho)$ is not dense.
            This proves the equivalence.

If $\mathbb E[\eta^{\otimes2}]=\mu^{\otimes2}$, then for every
            bounded Borel map $h:E\to\mathbb R$,
            \begin{equation*}
                \mathbb E[\eta(h)]=\mu(h),
                \quad
                \mathbb E[\eta(h)^2]=\mu(h)^2.
            \end{equation*}
            Thus $\operatorname{Var}(\eta(h))=0$, so
            $\eta(h)=\mu(h)$ almost surely. Applying this to the
            indicators of a countable generating algebra gives
            $\eta=\mu$ almost surely.

title: Proof
body_md:
The only measure outside the chord joining $P$ and $Q$ is
            $\mu_{-\delta}=(1+\delta)P-\delta Q$. The bound $Q\leq MP$
            gives
            \begin{equation*}
                \mu_{-\delta}
                    \geq\left[1-\delta(M-1)\right]P\geq0,
            \end{equation*}
            and its total mass is one. The remaining three measures are
            convex combinations of $P$ and $Q$. Thus all four measures
            belong to $\mathcal{P}(E)$.
        
            To prove the moment identities, we first verify that the
            weights cancel the constant, linear, and quadratic powers
            of $\vartheta$, while giving $-1$ for the cubic power.
            For each $i\in\{0,1,2,3\}$, construct the cubic polynomial
            \begin{equation*}
                p_i(\vartheta)
                    :=\prod_{k\ne i}
                        \frac{\vartheta-\vartheta_k}
                             {\vartheta_i-\vartheta_k}.
            \end{equation*}
            This polynomial equals $1$ at $\vartheta_i$ and $0$ at the
            other three parameters. Consequently, for each
            $j\in\{0,1,2,3\}$, the polynomials $\vartheta^j$ and
            $\sum_{i=0}^3\vartheta_i^jp_i(\vartheta)$ agree at all four
            parameters. Their difference has degree at most three and
            four distinct roots, so
            \begin{equation*}
                \vartheta^j
                    =\sum_{i=0}^3\vartheta_i^jp_i(\vartheta)
                \quad\text{ for all }\quad j\in\{0,1,2,3\}.
            \end{equation*}
            The coefficient of $\vartheta^3$ in $p_i$ is $-a_i$.
            Comparing cubic coefficients therefore gives
            \begin{align*}
                \sum_{i=0}^3a_i\vartheta_i^j&=0
                    \quad\text{ for all }\quad j\in\{0,1,2\}, 
                    \quad \text{ and } \quad
                \sum_{i=0}^3a_i\vartheta_i^3=-1.
            \end{align*}
        
            The identity for $j=0$ gives $\mathcal{M}_0(\Xi_{P,Q})=0$.
            For the remaining moment measures, expand
            $\mu_\vartheta^{\otimes j}$ by multilinearity.
            Summing with the weights $a_i$ cancels every term of degree
            zero, one, or two in $\vartheta$. Hence
            $\mathcal{M}_1(\Xi_{P,Q})=\mathcal{M}_2(\Xi_{P,Q})=0$.
            When $j=3$, the only surviving term is
            \begin{equation*}
                \mathcal{M}_3(\Xi_{P,Q})
                    =\left(\sum_{i=0}^3a_i\vartheta_i^3\right)
                        (Q-P)^{\otimes3}
                    =-(Q-P)^{\otimes3}.
            \end{equation*}
            This proves~\eqref{E: four_chord_cancellation}.
        
            Finally, the ordering
            $\vartheta_0<\vartheta_1<\vartheta_2<\vartheta_3$
            gives $a_0,a_2>0$ and $a_1,a_3<0$. Thus
            \begin{equation*}
                \Xi_{P,Q}
                    =\left[a_0\delta_{\mu_{\vartheta_0}}
                           +a_2\delta_{\mu_{\vartheta_2}}\right]
                     -\left[-a_1\delta_P-a_3\delta_Q\right]
            \end{equation*}
            is a difference of positive measures. Its Jordan negative
            part is therefore bounded by $-a_1\delta_P-a_3\delta_Q$,
            as claimed.

title: Proof
body_md:
We must construct a probability measure on $\mathcal{P}(E)$ with the
            same second moment measure as $\mathfrak G_\nu$ but a different
            third moment measure. We first average the perturbations from
            Lemma~\ref{L: four_chord} to obtain a finite signed measure
            $\Xi$ with zero total mass and zero first two moment measures.
            Averaging will also make its negative part dominated by
            $\mathfrak G_\nu$, so that a small positive multiple of $\Xi$
            can be added to $\mathfrak G_\nu$. Finally, we use a suitable
            test function to show that the third moment changes do not
            cancel under averaging.
        
            Since $\nu$ is not a point mass and is Radon on $Y$, choose
            compact sets $I,J\subseteq Y$ such that
            \begin{equation*}
                \max I<\min J,
                \quad \nu(I)>0,
                \quad\text{ and }\quad \nu(J)>0.
            \end{equation*}
            The partition function $Z$ is decreasing because $T\geq0$.
            For $a\in I$ and $b\in J$, we therefore have
            \begin{equation*}
                \frac{dP_b}{dP_a}(x)
                    =\frac{Z(a)}{Z(b)}e^{-(b-a)T(x)}
                    \leq\frac{Z(\min I)}{Z(\max J)}=:M<\infty.
            \end{equation*}
            Moreover, $M>1$: nonconstancy and nonnegativity of $T$ imply
            that $T>0$ on a set of positive $m$-measure, so
            $Z(\min I)>Z(\max J)$.
        
            Choose $0<\delta<\frac{1}{M-1}$, and use the parameters
            $\vartheta_i$ and weights $a_i$ from
            Lemma~\ref{L: four_chord} with this fixed $\delta$.
            This single choice ensures that
            \begin{equation*}
                P_a+\vartheta_i(P_b-P_a)\in\mathcal{P}(E)
                \quad\text{ for all }\quad
                (a,b)\in I\times J
                \text{ and }i\in\{0,1,2,3\}.
            \end{equation*}
            Thus the lemma supplies $\Xi_{P_a,P_b}$ for every pair
            $(a,b)\in I\times J$, with the same four weights.
        
            We now average these perturbations. The purpose of averaging
            is to distribute the mass removed at $P_a$ and $P_b$
            according to $\nu$ on $I$ and $J$, making it controlled by
            $\mathfrak G_\nu$. Define the probability measure
            \begin{equation*}
                \zeta:=\frac{\nu|_I}{\nu(I)}
                    \otimes\frac{\nu|_J}{\nu(J)}
            \end{equation*}
            on $I\times J$. For each $i\in\{0,1,2,3\}$, define
            $\Phi_i:I\times J\to\mathcal{P}(E)$ by
            \begin{equation*}
                \Phi_i(a,b):=P_a+\vartheta_i(P_b-P_a).
            \end{equation*}
            Since $\beta\mapsto P_\beta$ is Borel, each $\Phi_i$ is Borel.
            Consequently,
            \begin{equation*}
                \Xi:=\sum_{i=0}^3a_i(\Phi_i)_*\zeta
            \end{equation*}
            is a well-defined finite signed measure on $\mathcal{P}(E)$.
            Equivalently,
            \begin{equation*}
                \Xi(B)
                    =\int_{I\times J}\Xi_{P_a,P_b}(B)\,d\zeta(a,b)
                \quad\text{ for all }\quad B\in\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{P}(E)).
            \end{equation*}
        
            Equation~\eqref{E: four_chord_cancellation} and Fubini's
            theorem give
            \begin{equation*}
                \mathcal{M}_j(\Xi)=0
                \quad\text{ for all }\quad j\in\{0,1,2\}.
            \end{equation*}
            Since $a_0,a_2>0$ and $a_1,a_3<0$, the defining sum for
            $\Xi$ expresses it as a difference of positive measures.
            Using $\Phi_1(a,b)=P_a$ and $\Phi_3(a,b)=P_b$, we obtain
            \begin{align*}
                \Xi^-
                    &\leq -a_1(\Phi_1)_*\zeta-a_3(\Phi_3)_*\zeta\\
                    &=\frac{-a_1}{\nu(I)}
                        \int_I\delta_{P_a}\,d\nu(a)
                      +\frac{-a_3}{\nu(J)}
                        \int_J\delta_{P_b}\,d\nu(b)\\
                    &\leq C\mathfrak G_\nu,
            \end{align*}
            where
            \begin{equation*}
                C:=\frac{-a_1}{\nu(I)}+\frac{-a_3}{\nu(J)}
                    \in(0,\infty).
            \end{equation*}
            The final inequality follows because each restricted integral
            is dominated by
            $\mathfrak G_\nu=\int_Y\delta_{P_\beta}\,d\nu(\beta)$.
        
            Choose $0<\varepsilon<\frac{1}{C}$ and set
            \begin{equation*}
                \Lambda_\varepsilon:=\mathfrak G_\nu+\varepsilon\Xi.
            \end{equation*}
            Then
            \begin{equation*}
                \Lambda_\varepsilon
                    \geq\mathfrak G_\nu-\varepsilon\Xi^-
                    \geq(1-\varepsilon C)\mathfrak G_\nu
                    \geq0.
            \end{equation*}
            Since $\mathcal{M}_0(\Xi)=0$, the total mass of
            $\Lambda_\varepsilon$ is one. Thus it is a probability
            measure, and
            \begin{equation*}
                \mathcal{M}_j(\Lambda_\varepsilon)=\mathcal{M}_j(\mathfrak G_\nu)
                \quad\text{ for all }\quad j\in\{1,2\}.
            \end{equation*}
        
            It remains to show that the third moment measure changes.
            Take the bounded function $h=e^{-T}$. For $a<b$, the
            likelihood-ratio formula gives
            \begin{align*}
                P_b(h)
                    &=\frac{P_a\left(h e^{-(b-a)T}\right)}
                            {P_a\left(e^{-(b-a)T}\right)},\\
                P_b(h)-P_a(h)
                    &=\frac{\operatorname{Cov}_{P_a}
                            \left(e^{-T},e^{-(b-a)T}\right)}
                            {P_a\left(e^{-(b-a)T}\right)}.
            \end{align*}
            The denominator is positive. To show that the numerator is
            strictly positive, let $A,A'$ be independent copies of $T$
            under $P_a$. Then
            \begin{align*}
                &2\operatorname{Cov}_{P_a}
                    \left(e^{-T},e^{-(b-a)T}\right)\\
                &\quad=\mathbb E\left[
                    \left(e^{-A}-e^{-A'}\right)
                    \left(e^{-(b-a)A}-e^{-(b-a)A'}\right)
                \right].
            \end{align*}
            Both exponential functions are strictly decreasing, so the
            integrand is nonnegative and is strictly positive when
            $A\ne A'$. Since $P_a$ is equivalent to $m$, the
            nonconstancy of $T$ implies that this event has positive
            probability. Hence $P_b(h)-P_a(h)>0$.
        
            Applying~\eqref{E: four_chord_cancellation} to the averaged
            perturbation now gives
            \begin{align*}
                \mathcal{M}_3(\Xi)(h^{\otimes3})
                    &=\int_{I\times J}
                        \mathcal{M}_3(\Xi_{P_a,P_b})(h^{\otimes3})
                        \,d\zeta(a,b)\\
                    &=-\int_{I\times J}
                        \left[P_b(h)-P_a(h)\right]^3\,d\zeta(a,b)
                    <0.
            \end{align*}
            The strict inequality holds because $a<b$ throughout
            $I\times J$ and $\zeta$ is a probability measure.
            Thus $\Lambda_\varepsilon$ has the same second moment
            measure as $\mathfrak G_\nu$ but a different third moment
            measure. Therefore $\mathfrak G_\nu$ is not $2$-rigid.

\label{Ex: multiparameter_two_rigidity}
            Let $P_y$ be the law of two independent gamma variables with
            a fixed common shape $\alpha>0$ and rates
            $y=(y_1,y_2)\in(0,\infty)^2$. Put $P_1=P_{(1,2)}$,
            $P_2=P_{(2,1)}$, and
            \begin{equation*}
                \nu:=\frac{1}{2}\left(\delta_{(1,2)}+\delta_{(2,1)}\right).
            \end{equation*}
            We show that $\mathfrak G_\nu$ is $2$-rigid. The two laws have
            the same normalizing constant, so
            \begin{equation*}
                \frac{dP_2}{dP_1}(x)=e^{x_2-x_1},
                \quad\text{ and }\quad
                \frac{dP_1}{dP_2}(x)=e^{x_1-x_2}.
            \end{equation*}
            Both ratios are essentially unbounded.
        
            Let $\eta$ be a random probability measure satisfying
            $\mathbb E[\eta^{\otimes2}]=\mathcal{M}_2(\mathfrak G_\nu)$.
            Since $P_1,P_2$ are linearly independent, the completeness
            hypothesis of Lemma~\ref{L: moment_isometry}(a) holds.
            Its isometry $W$, with $S:=W\1_{\{(1,2)\}}$, gives
            \begin{equation*}
                \eta=SP_1+(1-S)P_2,
                \quad\text{ and }\quad
                \mathbb E S=\mathbb E S^2=\frac{1}{2}.
            \end{equation*}
            Here the almost sure representation follows from $W\1=\1$
            and the two values $P_1(h),P_2(h)$ of $K_h$ on the support
            of $\nu$.
        
            Nonnegativity of $\eta$ forces $0\leq S\leq1$. Indeed, for
            a realization with $S=s>1$,
            \begin{equation*}
                \frac{d\eta}{dP_1}(x)=s-(s-1)e^{x_2-x_1},
            \end{equation*}
            which is negative on a set of positive $P_1$-measure when
            $x_2-x_1$ is sufficiently large. For $s<0$,
            \begin{equation*}
                \frac{d\eta}{dP_2}(x)=(1-s)-\left|s\right|e^{x_1-x_2},
            \end{equation*}
            which is negative on a set of positive $P_2$-measure when
            $x_1-x_2$ is sufficiently large. Both cases contradict $\eta$
            being a probability measure.
        
            Therefore $S(1-S)\geq0$, and
            \begin{equation*}
                \mathbb E\left[S(1-S)\right]=\mathbb E S-\mathbb E S^2=0.
            \end{equation*}
            Hence $S\in\{0,1\}$ almost surely, with each value having
            probability $\frac{1}{2}$. The law of $\eta$ is consequently
            $\frac{1}{2}\left(\delta_{P_1}+\delta_{P_2}\right)=\mathfrak G_\nu$,
            proving $2$-rigidity.

title: Example
body_md:
\label{Ex: cmp_rigidity}
            On $E=\mathbb N_0$, take counting measure and
            $T(n)=\log(n!)$. The resulting family is
            \begin{equation*}
                P_y(\{n\})
                    =\frac{(n!)^{-y}}{Z(y)},
                \quad\text{ where }\quad
                Z(y):=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}(n!)^{-y}.
            \end{equation*}
            This is the Conway--Maxwell--Poisson family with its rate
            parameter fixed at $1$ and its dispersion parameter equal
            to $y$; see~\cite{ShmueliEtAl2005}. For every $y>0$, the
            ratio of successive summands is $(n+1)^{-y}\to0$, so
            $Z(y)$ is finite and positive. The statistic measure is
            \begin{equation*}
                \rho=2\delta_0+\sum_{n=2}^{\infty}
                    \delta_{\log(n!)}.
            \end{equation*}
            Set
            \begin{equation*}
                t_0:=0,
                \quad\text{ and }\quad
                \lambda_n:=\log\left((n+1)!\right)
                \quad\text{ for all } \quad n\geq0.
            \end{equation*}
            Then $\lambda_0=0$ and
            $\lambda_{n+1}-\lambda_n=\log(n+2)\geq\log2$.
            Moreover,
            \begin{equation*}
                \frac{1}{\lambda_n}
                    \geq\frac{1}{(n+1)\log(n+1)}
                \quad\text{ for all } \quad n\geq1,
            \end{equation*}
            so the reciprocal sum diverges.
            Thus~\eqref{E: exponential_MS} holds.
    
            Suppose that $\operatorname{supp}\rho$ contained an infinite arithmetic
            progression with initial point $a\geq0$ and step $\delta>0$:
            \begin{equation*}
                a+k\delta\in\operatorname{supp}\rho
                \quad\text{ for all } \quad k\geq0.
            \end{equation*}
            The gap in $\operatorname{supp}\rho$ following each $a+k\delta$ would be
            at most $\delta$. For $n\geq2$, however, the gap following
            $\log(n!)$ is $\log(n+1)\to\infty$, a contradiction.
            Corollary~\ref{C: exponential_rigidity},
            using the general sequence criterion, gives $3$-rigidity
            for every mixing law on $(0,\infty)$.
            Proposition~\ref{P: exponential_two_nonrigidity} shows that
            this order is exact whenever the mixing law is not a point
            mass.

label: Ex: discrete_gaussian_scope
title: Example
body_md:
\label{Ex: discrete_gaussian_scope}
            On $E=\mathbb Z$, take counting measure and $T(n)=n^2$.
            Then
            \begin{equation*}
                P_y(\{n\})=\frac{e^{-yn^2}}{Z(y)},
                \quad\text{ where }\quad
                Z(y)=1+2\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}e^{-yn^2}<\infty
                \quad\text{ for all } \quad y>0.
            \end{equation*}
            These are centered discrete Gaussian laws. Their statistic
            measure is
            \begin{equation*}
                \rho=\delta_0+2\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\delta_{n^2}.
            \end{equation*}
            Suppose that a strictly increasing sequence starting at
            $\lambda_0=0$ satisfied
            \begin{equation*}
                t_0+\lambda_n\in\operatorname{supp}\rho
                \quad\text{ for all } \quad n\geq0.
            \end{equation*}
            Write $t_0=k_0^2$ and $t_0+\lambda_n=k_n^2$, where the
            $k_n$ are strictly increasing nonnegative integers.
            Then $k_n\geq k_0+n$, so
            \begin{equation*}
                \lambda_n=(k_n-k_0)(k_n+k_0)\geq n^2
                \quad\text{ for all } \quad n\geq1.
            \end{equation*}
            Hence $\sum_{n\geq1}\lambda_n^{-1}<\infty$, and no such
            sequence satisfies~\eqref{E: exponential_MS}.
            Since $\rho(\{0\})=1$ and
            \begin{equation*}
                \sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{n^2}{1+n^4}<\infty,
            \end{equation*}
            Corollary~\ref{C: exponential_completeness_atom} also shows
            that completeness fails for some mixing law on
            $(0,\infty)$. Thus this family is outside the scope of the
            rigidity corollary. We do not know whether
            $\mathfrak{G}_\nu$ is $3$-rigid for every mixing law
            $\nu\in\mathcal{P}((0,\infty))$ over this family.

label: L: exponential_convex_representation
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The exponentially convex representation theorem
            \cite[Chapter~VI, Sections~20--21]{Widder} gives a unique
            positive measure $\mu$ on $\mathbb R$ such that
            \begin{equation*}
                F(t)=\int_\mathbb R e^{-\beta t}\,d\mu(\beta),
                \quad t>0.
            \end{equation*}
            Fatou's lemma as $t\downarrow0$ first gives
            $\mu(\mathbb R)\leq F(0)<\infty$. On $[0,\infty)$, monotone
            convergence applies as $t\downarrow0$; on $(-\infty,0)$,
            dominated convergence applies after fixing $t_0>0$, since
            $e^{-\beta t}\leq e^{-\beta t_0}$ for $0<t\leq t_0$.
            Continuity of $F$ at zero therefore gives $\mu(\mathbb R)=F(0)$,
            and the representation extends to $t=0$.

            Suppose that $F$ is bounded. If
            $\mu\left((-\infty,-\varepsilon]\right)>0$ for some $\varepsilon>0$,
            then
            \begin{equation*}
                F(t)\geq e^{\varepsilon t}
                    \mu\left((-\infty,-\varepsilon]\right),
            \end{equation*}
            contradicting boundedness as $t\to\infty$. Thus $\mu$ is
            supported in $[0,\infty)$. Differentiation under the integral
            for $t>0$ gives complete monotonicity, and
            $\mu(\mathbb R)=F(0)$ proves the last assertion.
