label: L: spherical_pair
title: Lemma
head: environment

label: E: pair_radial
title: Proof
body_md:
Invariance under $-I\in O(2)$ makes the characteristic function
            of the pair real-valued. Spherical symmetry and
            Equation~\eqref{E: definetti_characteristic} therefore give a
            continuous function $F:[0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ such that
            \begin{equation}\label{E: pair_radial}
                \mathbb E\left[\varphi_\eta(s)\varphi_\eta(t)\right]=F(s^2+t^2).
            \end{equation}
            In particular, $F(0)=1$ and $\left|F\right|\leq1$. Since
            $\varphi_\eta(-t)=\overline{\varphi_\eta(t)}$,
            Equation~\eqref{E: pair_radial} gives
            \begin{align*}
                \mathbb E\left[\left|\varphi_\eta(t)-\varphi_\eta(-t)\right|^2\right]
                &=2\mathbb E\left[\varphi_\eta(t)\varphi_\eta(-t)\right]
                  -\mathbb E\left[\varphi_\eta(t)^2\right]
                  -\mathbb E\left[\varphi_\eta(-t)^2\right]\\
                &=0.
            \end{align*}
            Intersecting over rational $t$ and then using continuity shows
            that $\varphi_\eta$ is real and even almost surely. Hence
            $\eta$ is symmetric almost surely.

            Put $r_\eta(u)=\varphi_\eta(\sqrt u)$ for $u\geq0$.
            For $u_1,\ldots,u_m\geq0$ and $c_1,\ldots,c_m\in\mathbb R$,
            \begin{equation*}
                \sum_{j,k=1}^m c_jc_kF(u_j+u_k)
                =\mathbb E\left[\left(\sum_{j=1}^m c_jr_\eta(u_j)\right)^2\right]
                \geq0.
            \end{equation*}
            Lemma~\ref{L: exponential_convex_representation} gives a unique
            probability measure $\lambda$ on $[0,\infty)$ satisfying
            \begin{equation*}
                F(u)=\int_{[0,\infty)}e^{-a u}\,d\lambda(a).
            \end{equation*}
            Let $\Pi$ be the image of $\lambda$ under $a\mapsto2a$.
            Then
            \begin{equation*}
                F(s^2+t^2)
                =\int_{[0,\infty)}
                    \exp\left(-\frac v2(s^2+t^2)\right)\,d\Pi(v),
            \end{equation*}
            which is the characteristic function of the law in
            Equation~\eqref{E: spherical_pair_mixture}. Uniqueness follows
            from Lemma~\ref{L: exponential_convex_representation}.
            Sampling conditionally iid from $\gamma_V$, where $V\sim\Pi$,
            gives a rotatable extension; Freedman's theorem
            \cite{freedman62} (see also \cite[Theorem~1.31]{kallenberg05}) shows that every rotatable extension has this
            form. Thus the rotatable extension is unique.

label: C: schoenberg_two
title: Corollary
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Necessity and uniqueness of $\Pi$ follow from
            Lemma~\ref{L: spherical_pair}. For sufficiency, let
            $V\sim\Pi$ be independent of an iid standard Gaussian
            sequence $G$. Then $\left(\sqrt VG_i\right)_{i=1}^\infty$ is an
            exchangeable sequence with the prescribed pair law.

label: R: tail_conditioning
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{R: tail_conditioning}
            The tail-conditioning proof of the extendibility criterion in
            \cite[Theorem~3.3]{mai20extendibility} uses invariance of the
            joint law of the initial block and the remaining sequence under
            rotations of the block alone. For a spherical pair this joint
            invariance can fail. If it always held, the argument would show
            that every exchangeable extension of a spherical pair is
            rotatable, which Proposition~\ref{P: sharpness} rules out. For
            blocks of length at least three, the joint invariance does hold,
            because Theorem~\ref{T: three-point-rigidity} makes the sequence
            rotatable. Among dimensions at least two, the gap therefore concerns exactly the
            two-dimensional case. The criterion itself remains true in
            dimension two, and Lemma~\ref{L: spherical_pair} proves it
            directly from the pair law.

label: C: gaussian_three_rigidity
title: Corollary
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Put $p_0:=\Pi(\{0\})$ and $U:=\eta(\{0\})$. The first
            two marginals of \eqref{E: gaussian_third_moment_rigidity}
            give
            \begin{equation*}
                \mathbb E U=\mathbb E U^2=p_0.
            \end{equation*}
            Since $0\leq U\leq1$, we have
            $\mathbb E[U(1-U)]=0$, so $U\in\{0,1\}$ almost surely and
            $\mathbb P(U=1)=p_0$. On $\{U=1\}$, $\eta=\delta_0$.
            If $p_0=1$, take $V=0$.

            Suppose that $p_0<1$ and put
            $\Pi_+:=\frac{\Pi|_{(0,\infty)}}{1-p_0}$.
            Subtracting the contribution on $\{U=1\}$ yields
            \begin{equation*}
                \mathbb E[\eta^{\otimes3}\mid U=0]
                =\int_{(0,\infty)}\gamma_v^{\otimes3}\,d\Pi_+(v).
            \end{equation*}
            Let $\nu$ be the image of $\Pi_+$ under
            $v\mapsto\frac{1}{2v}$. The exponential kernel with
            $T(x)=x^2$ has statistic measure $t^{-1/2}\,dt$ and
            satisfies \eqref{E: exponential_MS}. Corollary~\ref{C: exponential_rigidity}
            and the realization in Theorem~\ref{T: general_rigidity}
            therefore give, on the conditional probability space
            $\{U=0\}$, a random parameter $A\sim\nu$ with
            $\eta=P_A=\gamma_{1/(2A)}$ almost surely.
            Set $V=\frac{1}{2A}$ on $\{U=0\}$ and $V=0$ on
            $\{U=1\}$, assigning zero on any remaining null set.
            Then $V$ is measurable, has law $\Pi$, and
            $\eta=\gamma_V$ almost surely.

label: E: spherical_triple_generator
title: Proof
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $\eta$ direct an arbitrary exchangeable extension of the
            pair in Proposition~\ref{P: sharpness}. Put
            \begin{equation*}
                p_0=\Pi(\{0\}),\quad U=\eta(\{0\}).
            \end{equation*}
            The first two moment measures give $\mathbb E U=\mathbb E U^2=p_0$, and
            hence $\mathbb E[U(1-U)]=0$. Thus $U\in\{0,1\}$ almost surely,
            $\mathbb P(U=1)=p_0$, and $\eta=\delta_0$ on $\{U=1\}$.
            If $p_0=1$, this proves uniqueness.

            Suppose that $p_0<1$, and let
            \begin{equation*}
                \Pi_+=\frac{\Pi|_{(0,\infty)}}{1-p_0}.
            \end{equation*}
            Subtracting the endpoint contribution gives
            \begin{equation*}
                \mathbb E\left[\eta^{\otimes2}\mid U=0\right]
                =\int_{(0,\infty)}\gamma_v^{\otimes2}\,d\Pi_+(v).
            \end{equation*}
            If $\Pi_+=\delta_{v_0}$, Lemma~\ref{L: product_law_rigidity},
            applied conditionally on $U=0$, gives $\eta=\gamma_{v_0}$ on
            this event. Hence the rotatable extension is unique.

            Suppose instead that $\Pi_+$ is not a point mass, and let $\nu$
            be its image under $v\mapsto(2v)^{-1}$, so that
            \begin{equation*}
                \mathfrak{G}_\nu
                =\int_{(0,\infty)}\delta_{\gamma_v}\,d\Pi_+(v).
            \end{equation*}
            The Gaussian variance family of
            Section~\ref{SS: proof_three_point} satisfies the hypotheses of
            Proposition~\ref{P: exponential_two_nonrigidity}, since
            $T(x)=x^2$ is not almost everywhere constant. That proposition
            gives a probability measure $\Lambda_+\neq\mathfrak{G}_\nu$ on
            $\mathcal{P}(\mathbb R)$ with $\mathcal{M}_2(\Lambda_+)=\mathcal{M}_2(\mathfrak{G}_\nu)$. Put
            \begin{equation*}
                \Lambda=p_0\delta_{\delta_0}+(1-p_0)\Lambda_+.
            \end{equation*}
            Conditionally iid sampling from a directing measure with law
            $\Lambda$ gives an exchangeable sequence with the prescribed
            pair law. Its directing law differs from
            $p_0\delta_{\delta_0}+(1-p_0)\mathfrak{G}_\nu$, which is the
            directing law of the unique rotatable extension given by
            Lemma~\ref{L: spherical_pair}. Thus the new extension is not
            rotatable.

label: C: isotropic_app
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{C: isotropic_app}
            Let $0<\alpha\leq2$ and $k\geq1$, and let $\mu_{\alpha,k}$ be
            the isotropic symmetric $\alpha$-stable law on $\mathbb R^k$ with
            characteristic function $u\mapsto e^{-\left\lVertu\right\rVert^\alpha}$. If
            $0<\alpha<2$, then $\mu_{\alpha,k}$ has a unique infinite
            exchangeable extension if and only if $k\geq3$. If $\alpha=2$,
            it has a unique infinite exchangeable extension if and only if
            $k\geq2$.
head: environment

label: E: positive_stable_laplace
title: Proof
body_md:
Put $p=\alpha/2$. For $0<\alpha<2$, let $A_\alpha$ be the
            positive strictly $p$-stable random variable characterized by
            \begin{equation}\label{E: positive_stable_laplace}
                \mathbb E\left[e^{-sA_\alpha}\right]=e^{-s^p},\quad s\geq0;
            \end{equation}
            see \cite[Chapter~XIII, Section~6]{Feller}. At $\alpha=2$,
            put $A_2=1$. If $G_1,G_2,\ldots$ are iid standard Gaussian
            random variables independent of $A_\alpha$, then
            \begin{align*}
                \mathbb E\left[\exp\left(i\sum_{j=1}^d
                    t_j\sqrt{2A_\alpha}G_j\right)\right]
                &=\mathbb E\left[\exp\left(-A_\alpha\sum_{j=1}^dt_j^2\right)\right]\\
                &=\exp\left(-\left(\sum_{j=1}^dt_j^2\right)^{\alpha/2}\right).
            \end{align*}
            Thus $(\sqrt{2A_\alpha}G_i)_{i=1}^\infty$ is a rotatable
            extension of $\mu_{\alpha,k}$ for every $k$. This is the
            classical Gaussian-mixture representation of an isotropic
            stable vector; see \cite{CambanisHuangSimons} for the general
            elliptical framework.

            If the first triple of an infinite exchangeable sequence has
            law $\mu_{\alpha,3}$, Corollary~\ref{C: gaussian_three_rigidity}
            identifies its directing measure as $\gamma_V$, where $V$ has
            the law of $2A_\alpha$. Its $d$-dimensional marginal is
            therefore $\mu_{\alpha,d}$ for every $d\geq1$. By
            marginalization, uniqueness holds whenever $k\geq3$.

            When $0<\alpha<2$, Equation~\eqref{E: positive_stable_laplace}
            shows that $A_\alpha$ is nondegenerate, while
            \begin{equation*}
                \mathbb P(A_\alpha=0)
                =\lim_{s\to\infty}\mathbb E\left[e^{-sA_\alpha}\right]=0.
            \end{equation*}
            Its positive support therefore contains at least two points.
            Proposition~\ref{P: sharpness} gives a nonrotatable extension
            of $\mu_{\alpha,2}$, proving failure of uniqueness at order
            two. At $\alpha=2$, the pair law is $\gamma_2^{\otimes2}$,
            so Lemma~\ref{L: product_law_rigidity} gives uniqueness from
            two coordinates.

            Finally, one coordinate never suffices. If $Z\sim\mu_{\alpha,1}$,
            the constant sequence $X_i=Z$ is exchangeable and has the
            required first marginal. It differs from the rotatable
            extension above: in that extension $A_\alpha>0$ almost surely
            and $\mathbb P(X_1=X_2)=0$, whereas the constant sequence has
            $\mathbb P(X_1=X_2)=1$.

label: L: energy_space_localization
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{L: energy_space_localization}
            Let $F:[0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ be continuous, and suppose that
            $\rho=T_*m$ is locally finite and has full support on
            $[0,\infty)$. If
            \begin{equation*}
                \int_{E^2}f(x)f(y)F\left(T(x)+T(y)\right)\,dm(x)dm(y)\geq0
            \end{equation*}
            for every bounded real-valued Borel function $f$ that vanishes
            outside an energy sublevel set, then the kernel
            $(s,t)\mapsto F(s+t)$ is positive semidefinite on
            $[0,\infty)$.

label: L: canonical_laplace_support
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Suppose first that $Q_d$ has an infinite exchangeable extension,
            and let $\eta$ be its directing measure, so that
            $\mathbb E[\eta^{\otimes d}]=Q_d$.
            Lemmas~\ref{L: bottom_energy_localization}
            and~\ref{L: energy_space_localization} show that
            $(s,t)\mapsto F(s+t)$ is positive semidefinite.
            Lemma~\ref{L: exponential_convex_representation} gives a unique
            finite positive measure $\mu$ on $\mathbb R$ with
            $F(t)=\int_\mathbb R e^{-\beta t}\,d\mu(\beta)$ for $t\geq0$, and
            Lemma~\ref{L: canonical_laplace_support} places $\mu$ on
            $(0,\infty)$ and gives the mixture representation. A Laplace
            transform of a positive measure on $(0,\infty)$ is completely
            monotone, so $F$ is completely monotone.
 
            Conversely, suppose that $F$ is completely monotone. The
            Bernstein--Widder theorem \cite[Chapter~IV, Section~12]{Widder}
            gives a unique positive measure $\mu$ on $[0,\infty)$ such
            that $F(t)=\int e^{-\beta t}\,d\mu(\beta)$ for $t>0$.
            Monotone convergence and continuity of $F$ at zero give
            $\mu([0,\infty))=F(0)<\infty$, so the representation also holds
            at $t=0$. Lemma~\ref{L: canonical_laplace_support} shows that
            $\mu(\{0\})=0$, that $\nu_d$ is a probability measure, and
            that $Q_d=\int P_\beta^{\otimes d}\,d\nu_d(\beta)$.
            Conditionally iid sampling from $P_A$, where $A\sim\nu_d$,
            therefore gives an infinite exchangeable extension.
 
            It remains to decide uniqueness. The family $(P_\beta)_{\beta>0}$
            is in the setting of Corollary~\ref{C: exponential_rigidity}
            with $d=1$ and $Y=(0,\infty)$. Since $\operatorname{supp}\rho=[0,\infty)$
            contains $\mathbb N_0$, condition~\eqref{E: exponential_MS} holds with
            $t_0=0$ and $\lambda_n=n$. If $d\geq3$, the three-dimensional
            marginal of $Q_d$ is $\mathcal{M}_3(\mathfrak{G}_{\nu_d})$, and
            Corollary~\ref{C: exponential_rigidity} identifies the directing
            law of every exchangeable extension as $\mathfrak{G}_{\nu_d}$.
 
            If $d=2$ and $\nu_2$ is a point mass, uniqueness follows from
            Lemma~\ref{L: product_law_rigidity}. Otherwise,
            Proposition~\ref{P: exponential_two_nonrigidity} gives a
            different directing law with the same pair law; full support
            of $\rho$ ensures that $T$ is not $m$-almost everywhere
            constant. Finally, $Z(\beta)^2$ is finite and strictly positive
            for $\beta>0$, so $\nu_2$ is a point mass if and only if
            $\mu=c\delta_b$ for some $c,b>0$. By uniqueness of the Laplace
            representation, this is equivalent to $F(t)=ce^{-bt}$.

label: P: finite_independent_bounds
title: Proposition
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
(a) Write $\Lambda=\sum_{j=1}^{\ell}v_j\delta_{Q_j}$,
            where $\ell\leq m$, and realize $\eta(j)=Q_j$ on
            $\{1,\ldots,\ell\}$ with probability measure $v$.
            Lemma~\ref{L: moment_isometry}(a,b) gives an isometry
            $W:L^2(w)\to L^2(v)$ and
            \begin{equation*}
                W^*M^v_{\eta(h)}W=M^w_{K_h}.
            \end{equation*}
            Thus $m\leq\ell\leq m$, so $W$ is onto and $WW^*=I$.
            Multiplication on the left by $W$ gives exact intertwining.
            No independence assumption on the $Q_j$ is needed.

            The map $h\mapsto(P_1(h),\ldots,P_m(h))$ is onto $\mathbb R^m$:
            otherwise a nonzero linear functional annihilating its
            range would give a linear dependence among the $P_i$.
            Choose dual tests $h_i$ with $P_j(h_i)=\1_{\{i=j\}}$, and put
            $e_i=\1_{\{i\}}$ and $Z_i=We_i=\eta(h_i)$.
            Intertwining applied to $h_i$ and $e_i$ gives $Z_i^2=Z_i$,
            while $\sum_i Z_i=W\1=1$. Hence $Z_i=\1_{\{A=i\}}$ for a
            random index $A$, and
            \begin{equation*}
                \mathbb P(A=i)=\mathbb E[Z_i]
                =\left\langle We_i,W\1\right\rangle_{L^2(v)}=w_i.
            \end{equation*}
            For every $h$, $\eta(h)=WK_h=\sum_iP_i(h)Z_i=P_A(h)$.
            Applying this simultaneously to the indicators of a
            countable algebra generating $\mathcal{B}(E)$ gives
            $\eta=P_A$ almost surely, so $\Lambda=\Lambda_0$.

            (b) This is Theorem~\ref{T: completeness_rigidity}, applied
            to the finite complete kernel $(w,P)$.

label: R: joint_irreducibility
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{R: joint_irreducibility}
            For finitely supported $\nu$,
            \cite[Theorem~4.7]{VandermeulenScott} show that if the
            components are jointly irreducible, then $\mathfrak{G}_\nu$ is
            determined by its second moment measure among all random
            probability measures taking finitely many values. By Lemma~\ref{L: finite_competitor_reduction}, this is equivalent to unrestricted $2$-rigidity. Joint irreducibility is strictly stronger than
            \eqref{E: strong_localization}, under which Theorem~\ref{T: general_rigidity} determines $\mathfrak{G}_\nu$ by its third moment measure among all random probability measures on $E$. Under this weaker assumption the third moment
            cannot in general be replaced by the second; see the end of this remark.

            Let $\nu=\sum_{j=1}^N w_j\delta_{y_j}$ with $w_j>0$ and distinct
            $y_j$, and write $P_j:=P_{y_j}$. The components are
            \emph{jointly irreducible} if every probability measure of the
            form $\sum_jc_jP_j$ has $c_j\geq0$ for all $j$.
            Joint irreducibility implies linear independence: if
            $\sum_jc_jP_j=0$ with some $c_j\neq0$, then
            $P_1+t\sum_jc_jP_j=P_1$ for every real $t$, and a suitable
            choice of $t$ makes some coefficient negative. It also implies
            \eqref{E: strong_localization} for every Borel $B\subseteq Y$,
            hence for any countable generating $\pi$-system. Suppose
            $0\leq Q_\nu[f]\leq Q_\nu[\1_B]$. If $Q_\nu[f]\neq0$, joint
            irreducibility applied to its normalization gives
            $f(y_j)\geq0$ for all $j$. If $Q_\nu[\1_B]-Q_\nu[f]\neq0$, it
            gives $f(y_j)\leq0$ for $y_j\notin B$. If either measure
            vanishes, linear independence gives the same conclusions.
            Hence $f(y_j)=0$ for $y_j\notin B$.

            The converse fails. For the uniform kernel of
            Example~\ref{Ex: uniform_localization} with $y_1=1$ and $y_2=2$,
            the measure $2P_2-P_1$ is the uniform law on $(1,2)$, so
            $P_1,P_2$ are not jointly irreducible. Nevertheless $(\nu,P)$
            is strongly localized for every $\nu$. Here order two does not
            suffice. For $\nu=\frac12\delta_1+\frac12\delta_2$, the random
            measure equal to $\frac34P_1+\frac14P_2$ with probability
            $\frac45$ and to $\frac32P_2-\frac12P_1$ with probability
            $\frac15$ has the same second moment measure as
            $\mathfrak{G}_\nu$ but a different law.

label: C: finite_joint_irreducibility
title: Corollary
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Joint irreducibility means that whenever $\sum_i c_iP_i$
            is a probability measure, all $c_i$ are nonnegative. It
            implies linear independence
            (Remark~\ref{R: joint_irreducibility}). Let $\eta$ have law
            $\Lambda$ with $\mathcal{M}_2(\Lambda)=\mathcal{M}_2(\Lambda_0)$.
            Use Lemma~\ref{L: moment_isometry}(a) and the dual tests
            above to put $Z_i=We_i=\eta(h_i)$. Since
            $K_h=\sum_iP_i(h)e_i$, the same countable-algebra argument
            gives, almost surely,
            \begin{equation*}
                \eta=\sum_i Z_iP_i,\quad \sum_i Z_i=1,
                \quad \mathbb E[Z_i]=w_i,\quad
                \mathbb E[Z_iZ_j]=w_i\1_{\{i=j\}}.
            \end{equation*}
            Joint irreducibility gives $Z_i\geq0$, hence $0\leq Z_i\leq1$.
            Since $\mathbb E[Z_i(1-Z_i)]=w_i-w_i=0$, the $Z_i$ are indicators.
            Thus $\eta=P_A$ with $\mathbb P(A=i)=w_i$.

label: P: finite_block_bounds
title: Proposition
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $\eta$ have the competing law $\Lambda$. For a test
            $H:E^r\to\mathbb R$, put $K_H^{(r)}(i)=P_i^{\otimes r}(H)$.
            These functions span $L^2(w)$ by linear independence.
            Testing the order-$2r$ identity against $H\otimes H'$ gives
            \begin{equation*}
                \mathbb E[\eta^{\otimes r}(H)\eta^{\otimes r}(H')]
                =\sum_i w_iK_H^{(r)}(i)K_{H'}^{(r)}(i).
            \end{equation*}
            Consequently $W_rK_H^{(r)}=\eta^{\otimes r}(H)$ defines
            an isometry $W_r:L^2(w)\to L^2(\mathbb P)$ with $W_r\1=\1$.
            For $h:E\to\mathbb R$, set $B_h=M^\mathbb P_{\eta(h)}$ and
            $D_h=M^w_{K_h}$. Testing against $H\otimes H'\otimes h$
            at order $2r+1$, and using the spanning property, gives
            \begin{equation*}
                W_r^*B_hW_r=D_h.
            \end{equation*}

            In (a), realize $\eta$ canonically on the $\ell\leq m$
            atoms of $\Lambda$. The isometry gives $m\leq\ell$, so it
            is onto, and $B_hW_r=W_rD_h$ follows as in
            Proposition~\ref{P: finite_independent_bounds}(a).
            In (b), testing against $H\otimes H'\otimes h\otimes h$
            at order $2r+2$ gives $W_r^*B_h^2W_r=D_h^2$.
            The two operator identities and the isometry imply, for
            every $g\in L^2(w)$,
            \begin{equation*}
                \left\lVertB_hW_rg-W_rD_hg\right\rVert^2
                =\left\lVertD_hg\right\rVert^2-2\left\lVertD_hg\right\rVert^2+\left\lVertD_hg\right\rVert^2=0.
            \end{equation*}
            Thus exact intertwining holds in both cases.

            Choose $h_*$ so that $a_i=P_i(h_*)$ are pairwise distinct.
            Such a test is a linear combination of finitely many tests
            distinguishing the pairs $P_i,P_j$, with coefficients
            outside finitely many proper hyperplanes. Set $Z_i=W_re_i$.
            Intertwining and $W_r\1=\1$ give
            \begin{equation*}
                (\eta(h_*)-a_i)Z_i=0,\quad \sum_i Z_i=1.
            \end{equation*}
            These finitely many identities hold on one event of
            probability one. There, at most one $Z_i$ is nonzero, so
            $Z_i=\1_{\{A=i\}}$ for a measurable random index $A$.
            As before, $\mathbb E[Z_i]=\left\langle W_re_i,W_r\1\right\rangle=w_i$.
            Intertwining also gives $\eta(h)Z_i=P_i(h)Z_i$.
            Intersecting the events for all $i$ and for the indicators
            of a countable generating algebra yields $\eta=P_A$
            almost surely. Thus $\Lambda=\Lambda_0$.

label: C: finite_general_bounds
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{C: finite_general_bounds}
            Every target with $m$ distinct components is identified
            by $2m-1$ observations among competitors with at most $m$
            atoms, and is $2m$-rigid.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Suppose $m\geq2$. For $i\ne j$, distinctness gives a test
            $h_{ij}$ with $P_j(h_{ij})=0$ and $P_i(h_{ij})=1$, by
            subtracting a constant from a distinguishing test and
            rescaling. Then
            \begin{equation*}
                H_i=\bigotimes_{j\ne i}h_{ij},
                \quad P_\ell^{\otimes(m-1)}(H_i)=\1_{\{i=\ell\}}.
            \end{equation*}
            Hence the $(m-1)$st tensor powers are linearly independent,
            and Proposition~\ref{P: finite_block_bounds} applies with
            $r=m-1$. For $m=1$, one observation identifies the sole
            component among one-atom competitors, and two give
            unrestricted rigidity by Lemma~\ref{L: product_law_rigidity}.

label: L: finite_competitor_reduction
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{L: finite_competitor_reduction}
            Let $\Lambda_0$ be finitely supported and $k\geq2$. Then
            $\Lambda_0$ is $k$-rigid if and only if it is the unique
            finitely supported law with moment measure
            $\mathcal{M}_k(\Lambda_0)$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Only the reverse implication needs proof. Let $\eta$ have
            law $\Lambda\ne\Lambda_0$ with
            $\mathcal{M}_k(\Lambda)=\mathcal{M}_k(\Lambda_0)$. We construct a finite
            counterexample. No independence of the target components
            is assumed here.

            Put $V=\operatorname{span}\{P_1,\ldots,P_m\}$, and select
            a basis $R_1,\ldots,R_d$ from these probability measures.
            Choose bounded dual tests $h_j$ with
            $R_i(h_j)=\1_{\{i=j\}}$, and define
            \begin{equation*}
                T\mu=\sum_{j=1}^d\mu(h_j)R_j,\quad
                g_h=h-\sum_{j=1}^dR_j(h)h_j.
            \end{equation*}
            Since $TP_i=P_i$, every $P_i$ annihilates $g_h$.
            The second-moment identity therefore gives
            $\mathbb E[\eta(g_h)^2]=0$. Take $h$ to be the indicators of a
            countable algebra generating $\mathcal{B}(E)$ and intersect the
            resulting events. On that event $\eta$ and $T\eta$ are
            finite signed measures agreeing on the algebra, hence
            $\eta=T\eta\in V$.

            The set $C=V\cap\mathcal{P}(E)$ is compact in the finite-dimensional
            total variation topology: it is closed and every element
            has total variation norm one. Identify it with its compact
            coordinate image in $\mathbb R^d$, using $x_j=\mu(h_j)$; these
            coordinates are Borel measurable. For laws concentrated on
            $C$, equality of $k$th moment measures is equivalent to
            equality of the finitely many coordinate monomials of
            total degree at most $k$. Testing products of the dual
            functions gives one direction; expanding
            $\mu^{\otimes k}=(\sum_jx_jR_j)^{\otimes k}$ gives the other.

            If $\Lambda$ is concentrated on $\{P_1,\ldots,P_m\}$, it
            is already finite. Otherwise, let $x_i$ be the coordinate
            vector of $P_i$ and put
            \begin{equation*}
                q(x)=\prod_{i=1}^m\left\lVertx-x_i\right\rVert^2.
            \end{equation*}
            Its expectation is zero under $\Lambda_0$ and strictly
            positive under $\Lambda$. Let $\Phi$ collect all coordinate
            monomials of degree at most $k$, together with $q$.
            By Carath\'eodory's theorem, the convex hull of the compact
            set $\Phi(C)$ is compact. Thus the mean of $\Phi$ under
            $\Lambda$ belongs to this convex hull and is a finite
            convex combination of values $\Phi(x)$, $x\in C$.
            The corresponding finite law $\Lambda'$ has
            $\mathcal{M}_k(\Lambda')=\mathcal{M}_k(\Lambda_0)$ and positive
            $q$-expectation, so $\Lambda'\ne\Lambda_0$.
            The polynomial $q$ is only used to preserve nonuniqueness
            in this construction; it is not an additional observation.
